#3533. 5 Of The Best 4K Blu-Ray Black Friday Deals Under $20

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Admittedly, physical media isn't as big as it once was. Gone are the days where DVD sales could rescue a movie that underperformed at the box office. Sure, "Clerks III" got made because Lionsgate sold so many "Jay and Silent Bob Reboot" Blu-rays, but that's more of a one-off. Largely, the majority of movie fans are content to stream these days. But for physical media collectors out there, Black Friday is here. That means big sales on 4K Blu-rays.

If you're anything like me, it's a good excuse to break out the ol' wallet and spend some folding money on movies that have either been languishing on your wishlist or that you perhaps haven't even considered buying until now. Even for those who generally stream movies these days, recent HBO Max controversies serve as a reminder of why physical media still matters. Streaming isn't permanent. Digital purchases aren't permanent. Nobody can take away that 4K on your shelf (within reason).

Today, we're going to go over some of the best 4K Black Friday deals you can grab right now for under $20. From all-time cinematic classics to more recent gems, we've got a little something for everyone here. Let's get into it, shall we?

"Reservoir Dogs" may be the movie that put Quentin Tarantino on the map, but it was 1994's "Pulp Fiction" that cemented him as a superstar behind the camera. More than 30 years later, the quirky, violent, profane crime anthology is just as good as it ever was. /Film named it one of the 100 best movies ever made. It's arguably even better now since you can now watch it in crispy clean 4K Ultra HD. That makes it a fantastic deal during this year's Black Friday sale.

Going for just $16.99, it's hard to beat. The set also comes with a Blu-ray disc and digital code, which isn't always standard anymore. As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

The Prince and Princess of Wales at the awards ceremony

Over the past three days, William and Kate have been busy meeting about sustainability, innovation, transportation, culture, and relations between the two countries. This time, however, it was not simply a princess accompanying her husband on an official visit, but a woman who, after her illness and a long hiatus from major trips abroad, chose to return to her rightful role—and one the public has long expected her to fill.

The Prince and Princess of Wales with some Earthshot Prize winners

It’s worth noting that this is the first time in four years—since her illness—that Kate has accompanied Prince William on an official overseas mission. The last such occasion was in December 2022, when the couple traveled to Boston, Massachusetts, for the Earthshot Prize ceremony. Her participation in the trip to India thus reflects her desire to gradually resume her international role, as well as her awareness of just how important her presence is to the monarchy.

After her cancer diagnosis in 2024, Catherine prioritized her health and family, returning to public engagements without rushing things. However, her trip to Reggio Emilia, Italy, last May marked an important first step. The Prince and Princess of Wales at the 2026 Earthshot Prize ceremony

India, therefore, did not come as a complete surprise. The Prince and Princess of Wales in India

This refers to the project’s growth; since her last participation in Boston in 2022, it has significantly expanded its international reach and the impact of the initiatives it supports. “This year’s program in Mumbai promises to be the biggest and most ambitious yet, and she’s excited to see first-hand just how far some of it has come and meet some of the extraordinary people behind that success.” The spokesperson then recalled the couple’s previous trip to India in 2016, explaining that both have particularly fond memories of that visit. “The prince and princess are both really looking forward to what promises to be a fantastic week in India. They have such fond memories of their last visit together in 2016, and are excited to be returning a decade later.”

As mentioned, the most important diplomatic event of the tour took place on November 18 in New Delhi, where Prince William and Kate met with Prime Minister Narendra Modi. This was the only occasion during the visit when the royal couple left Mumbai, the city that hosted most of their scheduled engagements. Modi returned to the Indian capital specifically for this occasion after attending a major international summit in Manila, Philippines, to take part in the bilateral talks.

A spokesperson for Kensington Palace had emphasized the strategic importance of relations between the two countries, characterized by deep and ever-growing ties in numerous sectors, which include trade, investment, defense, security, technology, education, and culture. Kate’s presence alongside William during the meeting was considered particularly significant. “This meeting reflects the importance of that relationship, as well as the role their royal highnesses can play in celebrating and strengthening the ties between our two countries.”

“For the prince, it also represents another significant engagement as he continues to take on a growing role on the international stage. India, after all, holds a special place in the history of relations between the British monarchy and the Commonwealth. King Charles has visited the country numerous times, on both official and private occasions, strengthening a personal and institutional relationship over the years. For William and Catherine, however, this trip represented an opportunity to build a direct relationship with a nation destined to play an increasingly important role in the international balance of power.

A close-up of the Prince and Princess of Wales

With a population of over 1.4 billion people, India is now the world’s most populous country and one of the fastest-growing economies. Hosting the Earthshot Prize meant engaging a potentially massive audience on issues of environmental sustainability, resource conservation, and innovative solutions to combat climate change.

A beautiful image of the Prince and Princess of Wales

For William and Kate, returning to India also meant revisiting a country to which they are bound by personal memories. As mentioned, their last visit was in April 2016, when the Prince and Princess of Wales—then the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge—undertook an official tour of India and Bhutan at the request of the British government. During that trip, they visited Mumbai, met with representatives from India’s cultural and sports communities, and traveled to Agra, where they admired the Taj Mahal.

Right in front of the famous mausoleum—a symbol of eternal love—William and Kate sat on the same white marble bench where, 24 years earlier, Lady Diana, Princess of Wales, posed during a visit to India. That photograph of Diana, portrayed alone in front of the monument, became one of the most iconic images of her public life. Taken in 1992, when her marriage to Charles was going through a deep crisis, many interpreted it as a visual representation of her loneliness. In 2016, William and Kate’s decision to recreate that shot inevitably brought Diana to mind, adding a personal and symbolic dimension to their visit.

For Catherine, therefore, this trip is above all a new step on her journey back to public life following her illness. Not a demonstration of recovery to be celebrated as a race against time, but an opportunity to resume playing an important role while moving at her own pace. And to stand once again alongside William on a mission that concerns not only the future of the monarchy, but also that of the planet.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3528. Nicolas Cage's Acclaimed '90s Neo Western Thriller Flop Is Worth Revisiting

Nicolas Cage was more of a curiosity than a star in the early 1990s when he snagged the leading role in John Dahl's neo-Western/Noir "Red Rock West." He was squarely on the radar thanks to his standout performances in "Moonstruck" and "Raising Arizona" (not to mention, a coveted weirdo on the strength of his dynamic portrayal of Sailor Ripley in "Wild at Heart"). But could he singlehandedly sell a movie? Not yet.

Propaganda Films made "Wild at Heart," and the company's late co-founder, Steve Golin, shepherded some of the greatest filmmakers of our era from music videos/commercials to feature films. It wasn't always a smooth transition. Propaganda co-founder David Fincher, now considered one of our greatest living directors, got chewed up by the 20th Century Fox machinery while making "Alien 3." Meanwhile, music video veteran Antoine Fuqua delivered an aimlessly stylish dud in 1998 with "The Replacement Killers."

Stumbles aside, Hollywood prized Propaganda's director roster for its technical proficiency. Studios wanted a brand new wave of stylists who'd studied the work of Ridley Scott, Tony Scott, and Alan Parker. And Cage, the abundantly talented actor nephew of Francis Ford Coppola, seemed like an off-kilter star at a time when grunge rock and offbeat entertainment like "Twin Peaks" was catching fire. So, Dahl doubled down on the vibe of the moment, cast Lara Flynn Boyle (Donna from "Twin Peaks"), threw counterculture legend Dennis Hopper in as a villain, and had the makings of a sleeper hit.

Alas, like Dahl's subsequent noir thriller "The Last Seduction" (one of the finest of its kind), "Red Rock West" was shunted to home entertainment, which killed its Oscar eligibility and made it look like a misfire in spite of its sparkling critical response. It was anything but, and now, you've the chance to discover it.

"Red Rock West" stars Nicolas Cage as a Marine veteran who, having been bounced from legitimate oil-drilling work, winds up in the seedy, noir-ish kind of rural town where good work is available ... if you're willing to kill someone's spouse for a nifty life-insurance payoff. Sometimes, you just want to watch a mean-spirited neo-noir, and John Dahl brings the nastiness with dastardly elan. In this case, Cage's Michael Williams has been mistaken for "Lyle from Dallas," who's been hired by Kevin McCord (J.T. Walsh) to off Lara Flynn Boyle's Suzanne Brown. Lyle eventually arrives in town in the malevolent form of Dennis Hopper, and that's where the noir bedlam kicks into high gear.

Whereas most of the Propaganda Films directors were supreme stylists, Dahl was a classicist. "Red Rock West" and "The Last Seduction" were lean-and-mean thrillers — taut, sere, and brutally sexy. Dahl didn't traffic in the sweaty, sexual histrionics of "The Big Sleep," "Purple Noon," and "After Dark, My Sweet." Physical intimacy is purely transactional in his noirs. This might be why "Red Rock West" was relegated to home entertainment as a high-toned Skinemax film. It's the slowest of burns. It's like the Coen Brothers' "Blood Simple" without the flashy craft and cheeky sense of humor. Just know that this gem of a movie is out there, and it's so very worth your while.

#3527. Christmas in July? Why Stop There?

Why do we let something like the calendar dictate our holidays? The fact that Thanksgiving and Christmas are just four weeks apart means by the time you’ve returned from November family visits, unpacked, shopped, decorated, done the party circuit, bought gifts, and maybe—maybe—worked for a few days, you have to turn around and celebrate again. It’s exhausting and expensive and too warp-speed to feel like that much of a good time. I’m not arguing to ban Christmas—which I am using as a catchall for nondenominational winter holidays, however that looks to you—what I am proposing is, in fact, much more exciting. I think we should switch the dates of Christmas and Valentine’s Day.

Consider it! Instead of condensing so much effort and so much merriment into such a ludicrously small window at the very end of the year with nothing but the bland hell of winter ahead of us, let’s maximize our time by stretching it out. Valentine’s Day is for romance, whether that means watching Bridget Jones’s Diary with friends, eating overpriced meals at candlelit restaurants, making cards, or mainlining chocolates. So on December 24, celebrate platonic love with friends—à la Galentine’s Day, except we should think of a better name—and maybe go on a date on the 25th. If that date goes well: bam! You now have a plus-one to a New Year’s Eve party and a midnight make out partner.

If the holiday season has wrapped by February 14, the weeks following are the shoulder season. Life is slow. But by the time everyone trickles back home from watching Die Hard in their pajamas or shopping post-Christmas sales or going to the gym, you only have to survive one month until the sweet relief of spring in late March. Nothing makes more sense for how to survive the long nights and cold of winter.

So we go all-in on spring. Mid-April is when it likely won’t snow again; around then you no longer need heat—at least in New York City—so let’s make that a national holiday celebrating warm weather with seasonal bouquets (tulips, lilacs, peonies), foraged ramps, and maybe specials on dry-cleaning winter coats or sales on shearling boots.

But why stop there? We in America could take a page from France, where May can have four(!) public holidays as a kind of summer practice run. I’d be more than happy to celebrate VE Day in solidarity: Liberté, égalité, holiday! In our version, maybe botanical gardens will be free to the public for picnics. Maybe amusement parks will be gratis? Maybe lobster rolls and strawberry shortcake will be handed out on the street? Can the first summer blockbuster of May be an annual event with free popcorn? This month of long weekends will culminate in Memorial Day barbecues, which is a perfect bookend to summer with Labor Day—no notes.

Let’s keep summer luxurious, so summer Fridays will not be at the discretion of employers but mandated by the government for those three months. The Fourth of July can stay where it is with the caveat that if it rains, we get to observe it on the next day forecast for hot dog weather. Nothing important happens in August—phone it in, federal holiday or not. Labor Day stays, of course. The week following it in New York is Fashion Week, which runs concurrently with the US Open for tennis—very busy but very social. We’re going to adopt that nationwide as a festive season soft launching the country into fall.

And finally, let’s turn our attention to that somber stretch of time between early September and Thanksgiving. We don’t get enough time off, so we will move Presidents’ Day from February to mid-October for another much-needed holiday. Then cook a big turkey dinner on Thanksgiving, see your extended family, watch football, whatever, and delight in the fact that you don’t have to do it again until February. But start figuring out your Valentine’s Day dates now—those prix fixe dinners with chocolate lava cakes really book up fast these days.

#3526. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.

#3525. All Cheat Codes in GTA 6

The best part about any Grand Theft Auto game is the cheats, and Grand Theft Auto 6 delivers on that front. Rockstar's latest includes a whole mess of password-protected secrets that will really let you have some fun in Vice City. You'll have to work for them, though. GTA 6's cheats are deeply hidden, and will require you to jump through a few hoops to start using them.

Here's everything you need to know about cheats in GTA 6, from how to unlock them, to the list itself.

[Ed. note: We're still working to hunt down every cheat code, but until we find them all, this will give you an idea of what you'll need to do to unlock them all.]

Update (Nov. 21): We've updated this guide with inputs for three cheat codes.

If you're looking for a way to enter cheat codes the moment you start GTA 6, you're going to be disappointed. You won't be able to use them until you have fully cleared the story. Once you finish the game and return to your save file, you'll find a new Cheat tab. Open your Map, tab over to Progression, and scroll to the end to find the Cheats menu.

You won't get the actual cheat codes immediately. Each one is locked behind a requirement. That can be as simple as finding a specific car to earn the ability to summon it, or as demanding as having Jason and Lucia hold hands for four hours. Once you clear a condition, a pop-up message will tell you that you've unlocked a new Cheat code, and the unlock requirement in the Cheats menu will be replaced with the code.

Notably, your progress throughout the game, even before beating it, does contribute to these requirements. By the time you roll credits and unlock the Cheats menu, you'll likely already have a few of them unlocked.

To activate a cheat code, first pull out your phone by pressing Up on your D-Pad. Then hold down L1 and R1 on the home screen. (We have only been able to test the PS5 version of the game so far, but our assumption is that you'll need to hold LB and RB on Xbox Series X.) While holding those buttons, you'll have to enter the unlocked code with the D-Pad. Based on our testing, you won't be able to activate a code until you've actually beaten the game and unlocked the Cheats menu.

Note that activating a cheat code will disable saving for the rest of your play session. You also won't be able to earn achievements while cheats are on. Always remember to save before activating a cheat so you don't lose any progress.

GTA 6's cheats are broken out into five categories:

Below, we've listed every cheat along with their effect, unlock condition, and code.

Nitrous and fuel never runs out on vehicles

Discover the Interstate Ambulance in the Progress menu

#3524. 10 Best Directing Duos Of All Time, Ranked

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Most films treat the idea of the "director" with a dignified sense of reverence, especially since the end of the studio system. Where the producer's role was once seen as paramount in getting a film made and even in achieving a certain artistic vision, a film's achievements are now often attributed to the isolated decisions of the all-important director.

While we've talked plenty about the medium's great moviemakers — indeed, we already have a list of the 25 best directors of all time — it seemed appropriate to carve out space for the history's great directing partnerships. Though plenty of movies have two directors, the sustained union of two filmmakers over many years and/or films is rarer, and it warrants a closer look at the best of those recurring or long-lasting alliances. While the idea of the director usually implies one voice making the final decisions for the myriad creative components of a finished film, these directing duos prove that continuing that sense of collaboration into the chief position on a film set can bear rewarding fruit.

Here are the best directing duos of all time, ranked.

Jean-Pierre Jeunet and Marc Caro spent years honing their singular aesthetic in short films before making their feature debut with "Delicatessen," a pitch-black comedy set in a post-apocalyptic apartment building where a butcher-landlord keeps his tenants fed by turning unsuspecting newcomers into meat. Jeunet and Caro's penchant for grotesque faces and sickly yellow lighting helped make the film a sensation, earning it four César Awards, including Best First Film and Best Original or Adapted Screenplay.

"The City of Lost Children" saw them double down on their peculiar sensibility: a fable set in a decaying port city, where a prematurely aging scientist steals children's dreams and a gentle circus strongman, played by Ron Perlman, searches for his kidnapped little brother. Its macabre, nightmarish storybook whimsy remains one of the most singular visions in French cinema — an underseen, visually stunning masterpiece.

Then the partnership abruptly ended. Jeunet was tapped to direct "Alien Resurrection", and his subsequent films, most famously the candy-colored "Amélie," have generally been warmer and more polished. Meanwhile, Caro's lone solo feature, the sci-fi film "Dante 01," never found the same audience. It makes for a fascinating what-if, as nobody has quite matched the blend of cruelty and tenderness the two cooked up together, and it's hard not to suspect that the grime and the heart needed each other.

John Musker and Ron Clements met at Disney while working on "The Fox and the Hound," and they went on to become one of the studio's most dependable directing teams during its biggest creative revival. They made their feature-directing debut alongside Burny Mattinson and David Michener on 1986's "The Great Mouse Detective," a Sherlock Holmes riff about a sleuthing rodent, before Clements pitched an adaptation of Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid." Working with songwriters Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, they delivered a film that won Oscars for its score and for "Under the Sea" and helped kick off the Disney Renaissance.

"Aladdin" followed in 1992. The now-iconic musical was the highest-grossing film of its year and the highest-grossing animated film to that point, earning two more Oscars for Menken's score and "A Whole New World." The duo kept working through shifting tastes, with "Hercules" in 1997 and the sci-fi swashbuckler "Treasure Planet" in 2002, which flopped but has since found its defenders. They returned to hand-drawn animation with "The Princess and the Frog" in 2009, then made their first fully computer-animated feature with "Moana," which earned an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature. It also spawned a widely criticized, remarkably premature live-action remake — part of a trend the pair described as "bemusing."

The pair has since retired, closing out a partnership that lasted more than three decades. Their films were defined by the fundamentals of Disney magic: musical numbers that developed the plot and emotions, and humor that never smothered the pathos underneath. Few directors have made so many movies that feel so effortlessly designed for all audiences.

Before they set box-office records, Joe and Anthony Russo were comedy filmmakers from Cleveland. After their micro-budget debut, "Pieces", Steven Soderbergh and George Clooney produced their second feature, "Welcome to Collinwood." The brothers broke through on television, winning an Emmy for directing the pilot of "Arrested Development," then directing the pilot of "Community" and many beloved episodes after it.

That sitcom background is key to the work that followed in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, where their instincts for staging a dozen characters trading blows and punchlines helped define the quippy, ensemble-driven sensibility of their "Avengers" movies. However, that style has become a grievance among certain viewers who wish the films could escape their unrelenting sense of brand management. The brothers have cited François Truffaut and the French New Wave as major influences, but their biggest films operate within decidedly conventional blockbuster boundaries. Still, there's no denying the level of control needed to orchestrate some of the biggest hits of the 2010s.

Their post-Marvel streaming films, including "Cherry," "The Gray Man," and "The Electric State," have been considerably less successful creatively. But through their company AGBO, they also produced the far more inventive "Everything Everywhere All at Once." With "Avengers: Doomsday" scheduled for December 2026, the brothers are once again tasked with herding Hollywood's biggest cast into something halfway coherent — a feat they've proven capable of, against all odds.

Justin Benson and Aaron Moorhead work on the principle that a tiny budget and a big idea can take you a long way. They broke out with "Resolution," which premiered at Tribeca in 2012, a lo-fi two-hander about a man who holes up in a remote cabin with his drug-addicted friend while something strange lurks beyond the walls. "Spring" followed in 2014, a Lovecraftian romance set on the Italian coast that fuses monster spectacle with the heart of a character drama. Benson typically writes and Moorhead handles cinematography, but the two co-direct and often appear on screen.

That approach led to "The Endless," in which they play brothers returning to the cult they escaped. The film explicitly connects to "Resolution", establishing a shared cosmic-horror mythology. "Synchronic," their 2019 time-bending drug thriller with Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan, contains looser connections to that world, while the pandemic-era "Something in the Dirt" finds them starring as neighbors chasing a supernatural mystery.

Marvel took notice. They directed episodes of "Moon Knight" and much of the second season of "Loki," then helped rework the first season of "Daredevil: Born Again" before returning for its second. You could have worse pairs acting as custodians for one of the entertainment industry's biggest brands. Even if their Marvel work lacks the more personal flourishes of their smaller projects, you can still feel their indie-horror sensibility breaking through.

Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert met at Emerson College and built their reputation on music videos, most famously DJ Snake and Lil Jon's "Turn Down for What", before making their feature debut with "Swiss Army Man," an emotionally vulnerable absurdist comedy about Paul Dano befriending a flatulent corpse played by Daniel Radcliffe. The movie's surprisingly tender treatment of shame, loneliness, and the weird stuff that makes us human earned the duo the U.S. Dramatic Directing Award at Sundance in 2016.

That set the stage for their true breakout: "Everything Everywhere All at Once" cranked their style to maximalist levels in one of the decade's most unexpected hits. Michelle Yeoh's exhausted laundromat owner is dragged across the multiverse in a hyper-stylized, daffy yet sincere family drama about an immigrant mother and her daughter facing the potential end of the world. It was A24's highest-grossing release at the time — the studio's first film to reach $100 million worldwide — and won seven of its 11 Oscar nominations, including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Original Screenplay, plus acting wins for Yeoh, Ke Huy Quan, and Jamie Lee Curtis.

That made the Daniels only the third directing pair to win Best Director, after Robert Wise & Jerome Robbins and Joel & Ethan Coen. Though prone to hyperactivity, few other filmmakers could make a hot-dog-fingers gag and a mother-daughter reconciliation feel like parts of the same carefully calculated thematic throughline. Here's hoping their next film, with Matt Damon attached, sustains that momentum.

Phil Lord and Christopher Miller have built a career on finding inventiveness in projects that might have become franchise mediocrity under other filmmakers. The Dartmouth classmates started in television, co-creating the short-lived MTV cult satire "Clone High," before making their feature debut with "Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs," a frantic, silly adaptation of a children's picture book filled with surprisingly clever gags and character detail.

The duo kept pace: "21 Jump Street," a seemingly ill-conceived reboot of a 1980s TV drama as a buddy-cop farce, became one of the 2010s' most successful and acclaimed comedies. "The LEGO Movie," seemingly a feature-length branding exercise, became an inventive parable about creativity and conformity, launching a franchise of other LEGO films while transforming a bad premise into a cinematic miracle.

Their commitment to a distinct filmmaking voice also caused friction within the franchise machine, leading to their firing from "Solo: A Star Wars Story" late in production, though they went on to find other successes. As producers of "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse," they helped push the possibilities of mainstream animation forward. They also drew on their "Star Wars" experience in making 2026's "Project Hail Mary," a funny, meticulously crafted, heart-on-its-sleeve adaptation of Andy Weir's novel that has grossed roughly $685 million worldwide. The pair's irreverence remains central to their success: tongue-in-cheek self-awareness and a genuine love of subverting expectations have helped them turn unlikely premises into crowd-pleasers.

Lana and Lilly Wachowski came out of Chicago as comic-book obsessives, finding work as screenwriters before announcing themselves as directors with "Bound," a lean, sultry neo-noir starring Jennifer Tilly and Gina Gershon that showed off their formal command on a small budget. Then came "The Matrix," the iconic 1999 sci-fi smash that fused Hong Kong martial arts, anime, and heady cyberpunk philosophy into a defining text of 2000s action cinema. Its "bullet time" effects were imitated endlessly; it broke box-office records, and cinema was never quite the same.

But what really sets the sisters apart is how stubbornly they kept betting big. "Speed Racer" may have flopped on release, but it has since gained recognition as a forward-thinking work of art. Similarly, "Cloud Atlas" and "Sense8," their Netflix series about psychically linked strangers, have attracted devoted defenders of the Wachowskis' uncompromising vision. Even "Jupiter Ascending" has its champions. Their work has also invited a deeper reading of "The Matrix" as a trans allegory, something Lilly has discussed directly.

The sisters have pursued separate projects in recent years. Lana directed 2021's caustically self-referential "The Matrix Resurrections" on her own, while Lilly has been developing "The Hunted," a mid-sized thriller with an all-transgender cast. Even while working apart, both continue to follow the amplified, philosophical sensibilities that made their collaborations so distinctive.

Widely known as engineers of feature-length anxiety attacks, Josh and Benny Safdie were among the most exciting filmmakers working in New York before their broader breakthrough. They first drew attention with "Daddy Longlegs," a scrappy, semi-autobiographical portrait of a chaotic father that played Cannes' Directors' Fortnight in 2009. Then came "Heaven Knows What," a bruising drama about people struggling with heroin addiction, starring Arielle Holmes and drawn from her own experiences and writings. Their method of handheld close-ups, overlapping dialogue, and nonprofessionals cast alongside movie stars came together in "Good Time," in which Robert Pattinson plays a small-time crook losing control of one long night.

The apex was "Uncut Gems," in which Adam Sandler gave a career-defining performance as a gambling-addicted Diamond District jeweler hurtling through two hours of escalating bad decisions — a stress-riddled, darkly funny drama of street-level chaos and apprehension.

The brothers have since pursued separate directing careers, and differences in their sensibilities emerged in their solo work. Benny's "The Smashing Machine," with Dwayne Johnson as MMA fighter Mark Kerr, struggled commercially but revealed a quieter, more observant side of his filmmaking. Josh's "Marty Supreme," with Timothée Chalamet as a force of chaos, continued the streak of relentless havoc. Both films still carry the fingerprints of what the two built together: textured environments, tightly observed characters, and an acute sense of the worlds they inhabit. But the partnership that produced "Uncut Gems" remains one of the most electrifying of its era.

Few partnerships have been as productive or as generous to film history as Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger. Although Powell generally handled on-set direction and Pressburger originated many of their stories, they famously shared writing, producing, and directing credit during their peak years as the Archers. Powell, an Englishman who learned his craft on British quota quickies, and Pressburger, a Hungarian screenwriter who fled Nazi Germany, first teamed up in 1939. Pressburger later won an Oscar for the original story of 1941's "49th Parallel," and in the early 1940s they formed their production company, the Archers, whose films opened with an arrow striking a target.

That led to one of the great runs in British cinema: the wartime satire "The Life and Death of Colonel Blimp," the pastoral "A Canterbury Tale," the romance "I Know Where I'm Going!," and "A Matter of Life and Death," a fantasy about a pilot who cheats death. "Black Narcissus" won Oscars for Jack Cardiff's cinematography and Alfred Junge's art direction, while "The Red Shoes" remains an utterly dazzling film about artistic obsession, with its nearly 17-minute ballet sequence nestled inside a classical yet fantastical melodrama.

Their main partnership ended after 1957's "Ill Met by Moonlight," though they collaborated again on smaller projects, including "They're a Weird Mob" and "The Boy Who Turned Yellow." Powell's solo thriller "Peeping Tom" was so reviled by British critics that it badly damaged his career, though it has since been rediscovered as a masterpiece, thanks in no small part to Martin Scorsese.

Joel and Ethan Coen have long worked like one filmmaker with two heads, though Directors Guild rules obscured that for two decades by crediting Joel as director and Ethan as producer. The two also shared editing duties under the pseudonym Roderick Jaynes, a nonexistent editor who nonetheless earned Oscar nominations for "Fargo" and "No Country for Old Men." They finally received joint directing credit with 2004's "The Ladykillers." By then, the work had long spoken for itself: "Blood Simple" and "Raising Arizona" announced a pair of formalists with a wicked sense of humor, and "Barton Fink" swept Cannes in 1991.

Working frequently with cinematographer Roger Deakins, they moved between screwball comedy ("Raising Arizona," "Burn After Reading"), gangster pictures ("Miller's Crossing"), and Westerns ("True Grit") with unmatched formal and tonal precision. Few filmmakers could make movies as equally iconic as "The Big Lebowski" and "No Country for Old Men," works at opposite ends of the tonal spectrum that still feel unmistakably of a piece with the brothers' sardonic, philosophical sensibility.

After 2018's "The Ballad of Buster Scruggs," the brothers pursued solo directing projects, with Joel making "The Tragedy of Macbeth" and Ethan making "Drive-Away Dolls" and "Honey Don't!" But in October 2026, while receiving the Lumière Prize in Lyon, they said they planned to direct another film together. Joel's upcoming "Jack of Spades," which Ethan co-wrote and Netflix plans to release theatrically in fall 2027, is still a solo directing project, but their reunion comments suggest another collaboration may be ahead. Hopefully they'll add another movie to a remarkable joint filmography, which we've ranked in full.

After Ariana Grande decided to take a break from public life for a little bit, she recently came back into the spotlight for the premiere of Focker-In-Law. Whether the starlet is out and about or not, though, her music consistently plays across the airwaves. So what's it like for Grande to hear her work in public? Well, the Wicked actress got real about the wildest place she heard her music, and believe me when I say I was not expecting her to mention a bikini wax while explaining.

With the former Nickelodeon actress being one of the best-selling artists of all time and having ten Billboard Top 100 singles, she gets a lot of airtime. So it's pretty much a given that Grande would hear her own music now and then. As a matter of fact, when Harper’s Bazaar asked Grande about the wildest place she ever heard her own songs, she mentioned a wax:

Yeah, I was one time getting a bikini wax. And the song came on, and I didn’t think [the bikini wax employee] knew who I was at all. I never assume that anyone does.

Grande continued to mimic the satisfied look of the wax specialist, who also said to her, “And my kids love your show!” While the former child has spoken before about how fame tends to complicate her music career, it looks like it can also come with some surreal and somewhat funny encounters with fans as well.

A celebrity like Hugh Jackman can relate to the joy of hearing his own music in public. Months after his movie, The Greatest Showman, premiered, he recalled overhearing the film’s soundtrack as he was making his way to the door of an apartment or hotel. I can imagine it feeling like such an honor for an artist when someone is enjoying their work in some form or another.

Let's also be real, as Ariana Grande’s music is easy to love, given her immense talent. Per a fun fact about Grande, five-time Grammy winner Gloria Estefan spotted her talent when she was 8 years old and singing on a cruise ship. I think it's fair to say Estefan knows talent when she sees it.

Thanks to Grande's four-octave range and songwriting skills, she knows how to make her music fun and catchy. Back in 2019, her single “Thank U, Next” broke an impressive record, as it surpassed Ed Sheeran and Cardi B.’s streaming sales. And, this year, the “Positions” singer’s Eternal Sunshine Tour was her second highest-grossing tour she’s had, earning $107.9 million.

Now, on the heels of that top-selling tour ended in, Grande can celebrate her role in the highly anticipated Focker-In-Law. The film sees Grande play the fiancée of Greg Focker’s son, who also ends up having a rivalry with her future father-in-law. It’ll be exciting to see “The Way” singer go back to her comedy roots and mix it up with stars like Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro.

I wonder whether Grande's music was played on set and if so, which tracks were selected. Personally, I think a set seems like a more obvious place for her to hear her songs as opposed to a place where she can get a bikini wax. That aside, check out the Oscar nominee in Focker-in-Law when it opens on November 25th amid the 2026 movie release.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

There's no denying Andrew Scott delivered one of the most compelling portrayals of Moriarty opposite Benedict Cumberbatch in what remains one of the standout adaptations of Sherlock Holmes. The show ran on the BBC for 4 seasons, and fans are still holding out hope for a 5th run. I honestly thought this would be the role he was most recognized for, but it turns out that's not the case. Without hesitation, Scott told me it's actually the “Hot Priest” from Fleabag.

During a recent interview with CinemaBlend for his upcoming film Elsinore, which I think is one of the best films on the 2026 movie schedule, Scott spoke about portraying Ian Charleson, who is best known for his role in Chariots of Fire. I had to ask him which of his own roles he is most recognized for, and he didn't skip a beat:

Hot priest. Yeah, it's Fleabag usually. Maybe a bit of Ripley, a bit of Sherlock. A lot of the thing, because of NT [National Theatre] Live, which is a theater platform. Vanya is a play that I did, and a lot of people have seen it because of that platform… And that's the thing. Or else they just - they just don't; they just avoid me like, 'Oh, there's a dodgy person.'

I'm glad to see I'm not alone in this. For me, and clearly for a lot more people than I thought, Scott is the ‘Hot Priest.' He takes a man of the cloth and makes him layered, complicated, charismatic, and, above all, very sexy. If you've seen Fleabag, I'm sure the line “Kneel. Just kneel.” is burned into your brain for all eternity, just like it is mine. He clearly has a knack for making even a single line stick with audiences, as is the case with his one line in Saving Private Ryan.

Scott has a way of making normally unsexy professions seem sexy, all while making even a single line incredibly memorable. Recently, he was a guest star on a show called It Gets Worse, where he plays a therapist, so I had to ask him if people might start calling him 'Hot Therapist' now. Both he and Billie Piper weighed in.

Piper is spot on. I watched it, and there is no other word to describe that scene. But Scott is so much more than "hot." He is, in my opinion, a once-in-a-generation talent, and the roles he plays are memorable. He has this rare ability to make even the biggest performances feel incredibly personal, almost like he's speaking directly to each individual person watching. That's especially true in Elsinore. I think he's going to give Robert Pattinson a run for his money this Oscar season. Honest.

I'm sure people will continue to call Scott 'Hot Priest,' and he'll, of course, still be recognized as Moriarty when they see him. I secretly hope he gets 'Hot Therapist' thrown out occasionally now, too. With Elsinore hitting theaters on December 4, I have a feeling audiences might soon have another role to associate him with. And honestly, after this performance, I'd be surprised if Ian Charleson and Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, didn't start topping that list.

#3521. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#3520. Lesley Manville, Pierce Brosnan, and More Celebrate Violinist Joshua Bell at the Langham London

At the age of four, Joshua Bell was given his first violin, and he hasn’t put it down since. “I don’t remember falling in love with music,” says Bell. “Music has just been my life. I used to string rubber bands on my dresser drawers and make pitches by pulling the drawers out. I was fascinated with strings. It’s the closest instrument to the human voice. And I find it the most expressive instrument.”

Today, the Grammy Award–winning musician is one of the most celebrated classical violinists of his era. By 14, Bell was performing with the Philadelphia Orchestra, and would soon be touring the world. “I live in hotels 250 days a year,” says Bell of the nonstop schedule he has maintained since his teens. Specifically, Bell has been “staying at the Langham for decades now,” he says, referring to the regal central London hotel that first opened in 1865. “I chose it on my own because it was near one of my favorite halls in London, which is the Wigmore Hall. And now I stay with them whenever I’m traveling.”

That kinship was solidified over coupes of Champagne and hand-dived Orkney scallops, with the hotel celebrating Bell, a “Langham Luminary,” in its London ballroom packed with writers, artists, designers, and musicians.

Attendees included actor Simon Callow, House of Dragon actor Emily Carey, former British culture minister Ed Vaizey, Saturday Night Live UK cast producer Susie Hall, stage and television actor Indira Varma, and Verity actor Ismael Cruz Córdova.

Held in partnership with Vanity Fair, the evening marked the latest iteration of the Langham’s Luminaries in Residence program. The event series is continuation of the hotel’s legacy that brings together a diverse, influential community—an evocative reminder of prominent guests from its storied past, including Charles Dickens, Winston Churchill, George Orwell, Oscar Wilde, and Mark Twain.

“I’m not going to put my name in the same sentence as Toscanini or Mark Twain—who has stayed here, or Churchill, who has stayed here. But it’s cool to be part of the history,” says Bell. “So maybe someday, in a hundred years, there will be a violinist who might say that—that I stayed here. I don’t know, maybe that would mean something.”

It certainly does mean something. Pierce Brosnan and his wife, Keely Shaye Brosnan, “have been huge fans of Joshua for many, many years,” Brosnan tells me. “Keely went to go see him…I don’t know how many years back. Unfortunately, due to the LA traffic, she got there late, five minutes late, and they wouldn’t let her into the concert. So tonight is one of those nights.”

Bell, who performed mid-dinner with members of the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields—with a surprise appearance from his wife, soprano Larisa Martínez—brought about a collective catharsis.

Dazzling, fiery, and flamboyant, the experience of watching Bell up close is impossible to replicate. “I just think he’s incredibly soulful, and there’s something really elegant,” actor Russell Tovey tells me, before explaining how he actually discovered Bell via his Instagram algorithm.

For actor Lesley Manville, the event marked her introduction to Bell’s music. “I’m a bit embarrassed that he was not on my radar. But isn’t that nice to have a surprise like that?” says Manville. “Schubert’s String Quintet is one of my favorite pieces of music. It’s unbelievably beautiful. You think of a violin, you think of those strings. And it’s instant emotion. They just make you cry.”

There is a great power in being able to access the emotions of others, as Bell does.

“I think it is the ultimate gift to be able to make people happy,” says Brosnan. “My job is being an entertainer—to take the words of great writing and try to transform it into something that is meaningful and memorable.”

Speaking of entertaining, the week’s announcement that Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond was front of mind. “I wish him every joy and every success. He and I made a movie a number of years ago called Remember Me. I played his father. So I was very, very pleased and joyful for his nomination and now his success, and I believe he will be magnificent.”

And that creative full circle is exactly what the night was advocating. “Our own Luminaries in Residence program reflects our belief that meaningful hospitality creates genuine connection with extraordinary talents with one another, and with arts,” Bob van den Oord, CEO of Langham Hospitality Group, explained as he took the stage. “The Langham isn’t simply a place to stay, but a place to gather, exchange ideas, and indeed celebrate.”

#3519. Where to find the giant crab safe code and Crabshack VF5 SMG in GTA 6

Karkinos cannot be contained. Karkinos is free

Karkinos cannot be contained. Karkinos is free

Grand Theft Auto 6 has a giant crab haunting the swamps and, more importantly, the Crabshack VF5 SMG, a crab-themed gun, to help your future career prospects. It's all part of an optional event called Pelican Valley Outpost that sees you pick up the pieces of some questionable experiments carried out on behalf of a store chain. It's worth the trouble, even aside from the standout weapon. There's some cash to help reach your next family fund milestone and a free jet ski, too. Best of all, this little excursion is completely safe, assuming you don't run afoul of the local gator population.

Below, we show you where to find the giant crab in GTA 6 so you can clear the Pelican Valley Outpost and get the Crabshack VF5 SMG.

Pelican Valley Outpost, where the giant crab research facility is, has several codes you need to find on your way to getting the standout weapon. You'll find it on a medium-sized island southwest of the "Pelican Valley" name label on the map. Once you remove the fog from the region map, you can see it's one of the only islands in the area with buildings on it.

Take Jason's boat from his house, and set out. Definitely don't swim here, even if you're already nearby. There are too many gators for this to be a safe option. You can dock your boat at the boathouse and follow the jetty to the research facility proper. The boathouse is locked, but you'll get inside before leaving.

You'll see several buildings in the compound, but if you venture inside the first shack, you'll notice the power is off. You can still explore it, though you can't access the researcher's computer, which is essential for clearing the outpost. Head outside and around the back of the building near the blue crab cages. Interact with the breaker box to turn the power on, and head back inside. Ignore the computer for now, and take a right. There's a bag of chips in the kitchen if you want Jason to pack on some calories, and the login password for the computer is in the small bedroom opposite the kitchen. Investigate the small piece of wood on the floor to see all the choices, with "CLEAVES" being the most recent.

Interact with the computer, and press left on the direction pad to enter CLEAVES. You can skim through a few tabs of information on-screen, but the important one is the note in the green cell that says "Safe code = Double Success." Leave when you're finished.

Karkinos, the giant crab from the report, will jump you in a short cutscene, but you don't have to fight her. Press the on-screen button to push her off, and she'll vanish into the swamp.

If you want to get the giant crab safe code yourself, head to the research lab behind the shack next. There's a table with a trauma kit and some Zombix inside, which is handy, and in the specimen room you'll find Karkinos' former home and a list of experiments. Only one was a success, number 36. The code, "double success," refers to doubling the number of the successful experiment, making the code 0072.

Go back into the shack, and enter 0072 on the safe. Inside, you'll find a stack of money ($1,107 for us) and another note that reads "Emergency go protocol: 0212."

The emergency protocol is the boathouse code. Leave the research compound, return to the boathouse, and input 0212 on the keypad. The door will open. Karkinos' caretaker wasn't as lucky as Jason, but their loss is your gain. Pick up the Crabshack VF5 SMG from their corpse, and you can grab a bag of marked bills to drop off at Brian's lockup later, too.

You can leave the compound the way you came, or you can hop on the jet ski and make your way home that way.

#3518. Roger Ebert Preferred This Divisive 2007 Fantasy Movie Over The Lord Of The Rings

Roger Ebert wasn't as effusive about Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings" films as many other critics. For reference, Ebert gave "Fellowship of the Ring" and "The Two Towers" three stars (out of four) and then "Return of the King" three and a half.

"A true visualization of [J.R.R.] Tolkien's Middle-earth it is not," wrote Ebert of Jackson's "Fellowship," arguing it "adds up to more of a sword and sorcery epic" that loses the "innocence" of the books. Though, Ebert conceded in that review that "That 'Fellowship of the Ring' doesn't match my imaginary vision of Middle-earth is my problem, not yours."

Ebert subsequently wrote that the action of "The Two Towers" "would no doubt startle the gentle medievalist J.R.R. Tolkien." However, he praised "Return of the King" as a strong conclusion which solidified the trilogy as "a work of bold ambition at a time of cinematic timidity," even if he felt the film and trilogy fell "a little shy of greatness."

But you know what fantasy movie Ebert did love? 2007's "The Golden Compass," adapted from Philip Pullman's "His Dark Materials" novels. It's set in an alternate world where a piece of every person's soul exists in the form of an animal, called a dæmon. British orphan Lyra Belacqua (Dakota Blue Richards) embarks on a quest to rescue a friend and stumbles onto a much more cosmic struggle. Ebert gave it four stars, writing:

"'The Golden Compass' is a darker, deeper fantasy epic than the 'Rings' trilogy, 'The Chronicles of Narnia' or the 'Potter' films. It springs from the same British world of quasi-philosophical magic, but creates more complex villains and poses more intriguing questions."

While most would disagree with Ebert's quality assessment, he's onto something, as "Golden Compass" invites "Lord of the Rings" comparisons.

"The Golden Compass" was produced by New Line Cinema, the same production company behind "The Lord of the Rings," and it's clear the studio was hoping to repeat its previous success. "The Golden Compass" even features two important "Rings" alums: Ian McKellen (Gandalf) as the voice of polar bear king Iorek Byrnison, and Christopher Lee (the corrupted wizard Saruman) as a leader of the Magisterium, the Church of Lyra's world. It was reported in 2007 both actors were cast at New Line's behest.

But quite the contrary, "The Golden Compass" under-performed ($372 million in theaters against a $180 million budget), and sequels were never made. "The Golden Compass" even contributed to the end of New Line as an independent studio, as it was folded into Warner Bros. in 2008. Not helping the movie's financials was a religious backlash. The Magisterium allegorically represents all authoritarian religions but especially the Catholic Church, and "The Golden Compass" was in turn condemned by the Vatican.

"The Golden Compass" didn't win over fans of its source novel, either, due to abundant changes. The movie cuts out the book's entire ending, which directly sets up the sequel, "The Subtle Knife." But the attacks on religion? Those are taken right from the book. Philip Pullman is an atheist, and "His Dark Materials" is his rebuttal to the Christian-themed British fantasies of J.R.R. Tolkien and "Chronicles of Narnia" author C.S. Lewis, particularly the latter as both stories are about children traveling to different worlds. (Though Tolkien, for what it's worth, is said to have disliked "Narnia.")

"I cordially dislike allegory," Tolkien once famously claimed, believing it robs readers the freedom to interpret a work. For decades, said readers have since read into the influence of Tolkien's Catholic faith on his Middle-earth stories.

Sauron and his ring are a Luciferian conception of evil: A fallen angel who rules a fiery, molten realm and whose darkness spreads as temptation. J. R. R. Tolkien's villain is the Devil, Philip Pullman's is the Church.

Frodo carrying the ring echoes Christ carrying his own cross to Golgotha and, in turn, the metaphorical crosses that all of Christ's followers carry. "The Chronicles of Narnia," meanwhile, features talking lion Aslan as a direct allegory for the Christian God, Christ-like sacrifice and resurrection included.

In "His Dark Materials," the Magisterium worships "the Authority," a name suggesting an "authority" is all that organized religion is. The Authority is also a liar: He is not the creator of the universe, merely the first "angel" who came into being. The weak and withered "god" eventually crumbles into dust, as if humanity has no more use for him. The very last dialogue of the trilogy is Lyra endeavoring to build a "Republic of Heaven" on Earth.

Yet, circling back to Roger Ebert, he disputed the anti-religious reading of the "Golden Compass" movie, arguing it reworks the Magisterium into a more purely political villain, "a Soviet dictatorship or Big Brother." He specifically praised the film's themes as "murky," compared to Pullman's blatant allegory for the death of God, and affirmed that "the controversy surrounding ['The Golden Compass'] obscures its function as a splendid entertainment."

Amusingly, Ebert championed the movie for the same reasons many "His Dark Materials" fans rejected it. Toning down the anti-religion elements did not spare the movie the Church's wrath, either. One can only wonder what Ebert would have thought of the eventual "His Dark Materials" TV series that adapted Pullman's story to book fans' delight.

#3517. 10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest update isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

While you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Your Apple Watch's new Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

It seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

Now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

The new Find My app on the Apple Watch shows a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

After opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

The Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

The final weeks of Dancing with the Stars always feature really tough eliminations. However, the last few on the 2026 TV schedule have been brutal. Specifically, Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson went home during the semifinals after getting perfect scores for their Paso Doble and Glee-themed Quickstep. Now, co-host Alfonso Ribeiro has opened up about the conversation he had with the pair following their shocking elimination, and I'm feeling emotional all over again.

While Jenna and Harry were always at the top of the leaderboard and felt like frontrunners on DWTS Season 35, clearly, the fans wanted the other couples in the finale more. During a conversation with TV Insider, Ribeiro shared his thoughts on this, and the conversation he had with the pro and Glee actor after they found out they’d be going home. He said:

There was a lot of sharing of disappointment in my heart, what they did right, and just letting them know that I care and that I’m saddened for them. Or with them. I’ll leave it at that.

I’m also saddened for them. While Harry and Jenna always had some of the best routines of every episode, their DWTS journey was plagued by some controversy and intense online discourse. Of course, there was liftgate, which led to a comment from Johnson’s husband and fellow pro Val Chmerkovskiy that got him suspended from the show for a week. There was also the ongoing debate regarding the amount of dance experience Harry Shum Jr. had before doing DWTS.

However, while Jenna and Harry’s elimination hurt, and Ribeiro spent time talking with them about it, he also noted that no matter what the outcome, the last elimination was going to be painful. It’s the last one before the finale; it would have been heartbreaking no matter who got sent home, as he stated:

Going into the night, we know that all six of them … we’re going to break hearts with one going home. It wouldn’t have mattered whose name was called. There’d be controversy. There would be, ‘This is a shocking elimination.’ It was going to be that the last several weeks, no matter what, because this for the first time, I think in this show’s history, there were eight people who ultimately could win this show this season for many different reasons. And that’s not normally the case.

It does feel like the mirrorball trophy could be anyone's. They’re all pretty good, and it’s clear that everyone left has a very devoted fan base. So, it’s unclear who will win, and an argument can be made for any of them. I mean, when I think about all this, there’s part of me that wants Amber Glenn to win, and thinks she can do it based on her scores and consistency. Meanwhile, Connor Wood’s social media likes prove he has a very devoted group of fans behind him that could help make up for his lower scores and push him across the finish line. Seriously, it’s anyone’s game.

So, it made sense that Ribeiro said this in the wake of Jenna and Harry’s elimination:

There’s ultimate shock every time the person’s name comes up on that card, and also a bit of sadness. Because regardless of who you might think [should go] on and any of that, the reality is that they’ve all put their heart and soul into doing this. They put their lives and their families … they put it all on the back burner while trying to deliver these performances.

I totally see his point. DWTS is a massive time commitment, and it’s an intense experience both physically and mentally. These stars put their everything into it, and so it’s sad to see any of them not reach the end.

However, at the end of the day, this is a competition, and ultimately only one couple can win. To see who takes home the mirrorball, you can catch the finale of Dancing with the Stars this Tuesday, November 24, on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription at 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, as it will air live on both coasts.
