#3515. One Of The Most Unsettling Movies Of The '60s Is A Must-Watch On HBO Max

If you're tired of a mass culture that pumps out Harry Potter reboot series and Chris Pratt films so bad even AI couldn't generate them, why not revisit one of the great films of the 20th Century. Ingmar Bergman's "Persona" is currently available to watch on HBO Max, and offers a wonderfully confounding, disturbing yet lyrical experience that any film fan should see at least once. You're not going to have much of a clue about what's going on, but that's sort of the point.

The 1966 psychological drama was made following a bout of severe illness for Bergman, during which he was struck by a vision of two women slowly merging into one identity. "Persona" was the realization of that vision. It stars Liv Ullmann as an actress named Elisabet who during a stage performance suddenly stops speaking and moving. Her doctor advises she be taken to a remote seaside cottage to be nursed back to health. That job falls to nurse, Alma (Bibi Andersson) who in her frequent one-sided conversations with her mute patient reveals candid details of her own past. As their time together goes on, Alma and Elisabet begin to assume each other's identities.

Aside from urging viewers to feel rather than understand "Persona," Ingmar Bergman explained the film as a sonata for the instruments that were Bibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann. Andersson had worked with Bergman regularly since their first collaboration on "Smiles of a Summer Night" in 1955. "Persona" was, however, Norwegian actress Liv Ullmann's first Bergman film. Given the director's view of it as a "sonata" for the pair, it would seem the filmmaker was interested in his actors more than anything else.

But "Persona" is full of fascinating symbolism and is thematically rich enough that it's spawned endless critical analysis interpreting the film as everything from a modernist horror movie to an interrogation of acting itself as an art form. It's also been interpreted as an exploration of the distinction between our true selves and the masks we wear in social settings — which, considering the film's title, clearly has some relevance.

But even Roger Ebert admitted to not understanding the movie upon his initial viewing in 1967. When the critic revisited "Persona" in 2001, he still seemed somewhat perplexed, even while writing, "I know most of what I am ever likely to know about films, and I think I understand that the best approach to 'Persona' is a literal one." The ending of "Persona" certainly offers no answers, but it's not supposed to. Susan Sontag wrote that "Persona" is "bound to trouble, perplex and frustrate most filmgoers," and it does — but in the most beautiful, mesmeric, and disturbing way possible. The film is streaming on HBO Max at the time of writing, but can also be found on the usual digital platforms as well as on archive.org for free.

#3514. I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says users accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly quickly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

The new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says users identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Out of the bigger AI chatbots out there, Grok is very much the worst at protecting minors. It can be accessed through X or as its own standalone app, and while its terms of use indicate there's a minimum age requirement of 13, a recent report by Common Sense Media says the platform's age checks aren't effective.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence."

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide users towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

#3513. Are the Royals More Relatable Now Than Ever?

Prince William and Kate Middleton’s visit to India for the Earthshot Prize ceremony marked their first joint overseas tour in four years, and the couple used it as an opportunity to demonstrate their star power. Through their action-packed itinerary, which took them from Mumbai to New Delhi, the Prince and Princess of Wales have paved the way for a new style of royal tour.

From Kate unexpectedly presenting an award and delivering a speech at the star-studded Earthshot Prize event to her and William playing cricket and traveling around Mumbai in an electric rickshaw, there have been plenty of photo opportunities and headlines around the world about the environmental initiative William is so passionate about.

According to royals author Russell Myers, who followed the couple on tour, the speech Kate gave at the awards was kept top secret. “None of us knew she was presenting an award on the night, or that she was going to speak. The auditorium was packed. There were about 5,000 people there. It’s been the biggest Earthshot yet, and you could see Catherine was nervous, but she delivered an absolutely brilliant speech. I’d say her best yet.

“It’s been wonderful for her to be here, supporting William, and you can see they’ve really had fun. Because of ongoing terror threats, there have been less walkabouts, but it’s been a very successful and varied tour, and I think, being shorter than most tours, it sets a new blueprint when it comes to royal tours for the couple in the future.”

Prince William and Princess Kate arrive to attend the Earthshot Prize awards night at the Jio World Convention Centre on November 17, 2026 in Mumbai, India.

There are seemingly already plans for another royal tour, says Myers.

“William let slip that Australia is on the cards next, and if that’s the case, I imagine they will go as a family. They don’t want to be away from their children for too long, and what a way it would be to win support for the monarchy Down Under,” Myers says.

According to royals insiders, there had been some nervousness around the trip after the couple’s disastrous tour of the Caribbean in March 2022, when their visit was overshadowed by calls for the UK to apologize for slavery. Then some of their photo calls, including one that involved the couple riding in an open-top Land Rover, led to accusations of the royals appearing colonial and out of touch.

“I think there has been a slight nervousness about how this tour would be received, but the reception has been really good,” Myers says. “The fact that William and Catherine have included a visit to New Delhi to see Prime Minister Modi is a clever move. While this is a private trip to promote Earthshot, the Foreign Office was keen for William to meet with the Indian prime minister, so they have packed that into the itinerary too.”

The visit to India has come at a time when the royals are on something of a charm offensive following a difficult year for the royal family, from Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest to what one palace insider calls “the ongoing soap opera” with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. (Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has not been charged and has denied all allegations of wrongdoing.)

William and Kate are keen to carve out their own initiatives and projects focusing on their major priorities, including the environment, children’s early years, and mental health. With the challenge of having Harry and Meghan carrying out their own engagements, the Prince and Princess of Wales have been careful to establish clear parameters that set them apart as working royals. In one telling moment while on an engagement in Mumbai, Kate was asked for an autograph. She politely declined, so as not to breach protocol, a clear contrast to the Duchess of Sussex, who has signed autographs in the past.

“Catherine was asked to sign an autograph, but she was right not to. It wasn’t a snub; it was just adhering to protocol. An autograph could be sold for money,” notes Dickie Arbiter, former press secretary to Queen Elizabeth II.

According to author Tom Bower, the royals are more relatable now than they were during the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, who famously never gave a press interview. In recent weeks, Prince William has appeared as a guest on The Graham Norton Show (to promote Earthshot), and he’s revealed how he drinks his cider and his love of wild swimming as part of his guest-editing stint for a recent issue of Country Life magazine.

“The royals are more relatable, perhaps, than they ever have been, but they are not celebrities. There’s a danger of being too relatable, too much ‘one of the people,’ which means they can lose some of their mystery,” Bower says.

“William will have been advised to do TV appearances and take on media opportunities to bolster his public image. Of course, it’s charming to hear these nuggets and see this side of the prince, but I do think there’s a need to see and hear more from William about his broader plans. Over the years, Charles has made huge efforts to appeal to all cultural aspects of society. I’m not sure William has done that. He’s got to find a way of connecting with everyone, not just the younger generation,” Bower adds.

The Earthshot Prize awards have been a powerful way of demonstrating that William doesn’t just talk the talk; he is insisting on action.

“The Earthshot is a master class in what needs to be done,” concludes Arbiter. “He’s pushing for environmental issues and climate change, and he’s getting people to do something about it. The fact that he is so well supported, and by so many high-profile people, shows his pulling power and influence.”

#3512. GTA 6 Players Are Obsessed With Finding IRL Florida in Vice City

Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is in the wild, one thing has become clear: The open-world crime stuff is secondary. This thing's a life sim. GTA 6's life sim bona fides are so undeniable that, within the first two days of its release, a not-insignificant swath of players have eschewed the elaborate robberies and high-tension shootouts to instead embrace the ancient gaming tradition of "finding IRL locations and Leo memeing at them."

Players of reality-inspired open-world games have always done this, whether it's finding the Bean in Watch Dogs' version of Chicago or visiting the John Wick hotel in DLC for The Division 2. But with GTA 6, which takes place in a satirized version of Florida called Leonida, players were always going to take it to another level. This game is from Rockstar Games, a studio so well-known for its attention to detail it once infamously implemented horse testicles that shrink in reaction to cold weather. GTA 6 has been in development for a decade. Its leads have conducted "research" trips to Miami-Dade County for just as long. A perfect storm for some ridiculously faithful world design that's resulted in brain-melting levels of realism.

GTA 6's realistic visuals have changed the way I play

What's most remarkable is that Rockstar's attention to detail isn't just limited to reimagining iconic Miami landmarks like the Adrienne Arsht Center or the E11EVEN nightclub, though the game does have those. It's also found in recreations of nondescript buildings you'd otherwise never think twice about. This design ethos is best illustrated in one viral clip in which an unidentified creator films Jason walking through an apartment complex before coming to a stop on a patio overlooking a South Beach meridian. The creator, continuing to film, stands up in real life, then walks out of their own front door and onto a patio of the same exact building. ("This is crazy [exploding head emoji]," they wrote. "My apartment is in a video game.")

Even in the realm of sports, Rockstar wasn't just drawn to the major leagues. Yes, GTA 6 includes a riff on Miami's Kaseya Cener (homebase of the Miami Heat), but it also includes a pixel-perfect facsimile of the Miami Marine Stadium. Built in the early '60s as a regatta venue, the stadium went on to host film shoots, presidential rallies, and concerts from the likes of Queen, The Who, Jimmy Buffet, and other megawatt stars, according to the nonprofit Restore Miami Marine Stadium. Then, in 1992, Hurricane Andrew took the venue out of commission. It's spent the past three decades collecting rust and graffiti. But in GTA 6, it's just...there. (In August of this year, Miami voters passed a referendum that paves the way for a potential restoration.)

Fans have been unpacking these references throughout the entirety of GTA 6's marketing cycle. Following Rockstar's release of the second GTA 6 trailer, back in May 2025, I could've sworn — based on a vanishingly brief 0.5-second glance — that the South Beach party spot The Clevelander would serve as a location in the game. The bar's marketing department never responded to my initial request for comment. Now that I've played, I can confirm that, yes, it's absolutely in the game, in all its flamingo-pink glory. The Clevelander is somewhat of an institution, having remained a South Beach party spot for decades on the back of some extremely lucky local ordinances, but at face value, it's not all that distinct from any other South Beach bar: neon lights, a questionable pool, overpriced drinks. And yet, it's in GTA 6 too.

The locations GTA 6 players seem drawn to point out tend to be in the Miami metropolitan area, which makes sense: It's the population nexus of the state. But Vice City encompasses a small portion of Leonida's map, and Florida itself poses no shortage of things to reference beyond the Miami-Dade County limits. Who knows what players will find and Leo meme at? Though there's one thing not worth seeking out. In its quest to construct an alternate reality, Rockstar neglected to include arguably the most Florida landmark of them: Disney World.

Rockstar steers clear of the house of mouse

He loved the sport, but he hated what it was doing to him, so he moved to the broadcast booth.

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

The Traitors: New Blood returns for a second season in 2027. I am excited because I gladly welcome any Traitors. However, New Blood may be my least favorite of the franchise.

It’s not necessarily a bad show, but it doesn’t seem to understand how to present itself in a more appealing package. As a Traitors superfan, that's made it extra frustrating to watch. Nonetheless, all hope isn’t lost, and I have some suggestions.

Warning: The Traitors: New Blood spoilers are ahead. Proceed with caution

For a long time, people used cliffhangers to entice readers or viewers to continuously return. It’s been part of the reality TV landscape for many decades. However, it’s not the only way to ensure viewership. The original The Traitors uses cliffhangers quite often, but it never felt as tedious as it does on The Traitors: New Blood.

This could be because many of the other versions aren’t using a one-episode-a-week format. They either drop multiple episodes weekly or many on one day. Usually, Peacock’s version, for at least a few weeks, releases more than one episode weekly.. The Traitors: New Blood starts this way, but eventually shifts to one episode a week.

The switch is ultimately when the cliffhangers start to feel excessive. The episodes feel like a lot of nothing happens just to rush a cliffhanger ending. The end doesn’t have to be stuffed with cliffhangers. New Blood either needs longer episodes to flesh out the story better, or multiple episodes per week.

A major appeal of The Traitors US is that it’s full of familiar faces. We know these reality TV stars, so we can get excited to see what they bring to the show. The Traitors: New Blood has some familiar influencers, but they are not as recognizable as reality TV stars and celebrities. Therefore, we want to get to know them.

New Blood didn’t showcase these players well. Victor and the Traitors stood out the most, but I wanted to get to know everyone a little bit. I wanted more rooting interest and people I want to see again on other reality TV shows. Season 2 needs a better balance of highlighting various personalities.

Fruitgate starts very interestingly and produced one of the season’s best episodes. However, the constant talk about it made me grow sour about the topic. It made me question if it’s fair that the Traitors have to make so many risky moves.

The murders in plain sight have never bothered me before. They’re fun. However, New Blood’s version felt like it set the Traitors up for failure. I don’t want to lose that element of the show, but maybe it’s time to revamp it because having someone hand someone a fruit out of the blue feels too obvious.

The Traitors: Canada Season 4 has a subtle version of this. The Traitors just have to bring a bowl of strawberries to breakfast. They don’t have to do anything but slightly encourage a few people to eat them.

I still have faith in The Traitors: New Blood; I just think the producers need to reevaluate the show and not misunderstand why it isn’t working for many dedicated fans.

Stream The Traitors: New Blood on Peacock.

#3508. This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur

Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unpredictable; when I went there this summer for lunch with a movie producer, we spotted a powerful name-brand media executive, an architectural bigwig who designs the homes of billionaires, and a two-time Academy Award–winning actor. A few nights later, I sat near Walter Isaacson, who’s a regular. And don’t just take it from Elon Musk’s biographer. Matthew Schneier, the chief restaurant critic at New York magazine, recently named Borgo the city’s best all-around restaurant.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

On one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades. He met Ross Bleckner there, and David Salle. He used to have a massive loft studio in Williamsburg, but as rents went up, he moved deeper into Brooklyn, to Fort Greene, where he built a studio in his basement.

The twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art. That’s because he was Andrew Tarlow—the painter and restaurateur who kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic with his restaurant Diner and, yes, also owns Borgo.

After launching that instant hit in an old, reclaimed diner, Tarlow opened five more era-defining Brooklyn spots before finally venturing into Manhattan with Borgo. All along, he’s still been the artist who got a job at The Odeon so that he could meet his heroes. He’s still painting away in his brownstone, doodling on notepads during concept meetings. He’s had shows recently at galleries such as Tiwa Select; he’s loosely associated with the Galerie Sardine extended universe; and he’s someone whose work I’ve been told about for years by those in the know.

As they put it, Tarlow is an emerging artist who happens to own the best all-around restaurant in Manhattan, as well as a bunch of other successful spots in Brooklyn.

“I realized, opening Borgo, that I really loved working in restaurants—and not that I had forgotten, but I hadn’t actually worked services in a while until I opened,” Tarlow told me during a studio visit. “And then, in a similar way, I think—I love making paintings. I actually will paint forever, no matter what happens.”

The studio had dozens of unstretched canvases heaped on the ground, some still rolled up, and others hanging via a pin on the studio wall. They showed figures grappling with pain in fierce color-blocked fields, automatic-painting abstractions, faces fading into other faces. One painting was a portrait of the artist Joe Bradley, a friend.

The studio is in the basement of the Fort Greene brownstone where Tarlow has lived for two decades with his wife, Kate Huling, raising four kids in a kind of neo-boho paradise. There were no studio assistants, no art handlers, no frames, no boxes, no packaging—just the artist and the work.

“It was kind of just as chaotic as everything else there, but in the most perfect warm embrace of a way. I saw the pure energy that he put into his paintings and the stories that they told,” says Alex Tieghi-Walker, the founder of Tiwa Select, calling from London. “So many artists could be quite—rightfully so, but quite precious with their works. And I love that Andrew was just like, ‘Oh, pull out the ones you’re taking and just take them in an Uber home.’”

Tarlow grabbed at a canvas bare-handed, one with a bit of a conceptual bent, and put it up on an easel.

“I’ve had this up on the wall for a while now, and I just continued to look at it because I’m happy with it. I’m also a little unsettled—I mean, I’m showing you the inside of my drawers. I’m also a little unsettled by how far it’s gone abstract-wise.”

He told me he couldn’t really do his other job, the restaurant job, without painting at odd hours. They’re totally separate, but complementary in a cosmic way.

“What are the processes? Like you said, for some people, it’s nine to five. Then you listen to the news, smoke a cigarette, drink coffee. It’s either working or it’s not. The door either opens or it’s not,” Tarlow said, gesturing around to his studio. “But I’m going to go here every day, and I’m going to push some paint on canvas.”

Diner opened in 1999, a few years after Tarlow moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg—where the crumbling street dead-ends into the East River. While looking for a cheap studio space, he found a 6,000-square-foot loft across the street from an abandoned diner from the 1920s. The loft’s landlord bought the diner, and in 1999, Tarlow opened Diner with then partner Mark Firth—and watched as it was patronized by only the artists across the street.

“You could stand outside the restaurant in those days and not see a single person walk by,” he told Bon Appetit in 2010.

Tarlow kept expanding. He opened Marlow & Sons, and then the butcher shop and specialty food store Marlow & Daughters. He founded a bakery, She Wolf, and a literary magazine, Diner Journal. He operated the restaurant at the Wythe Hotel, but only for a few years. Instead of doing the easy thing, Vegas-ifying Diner in some new development on the Williamsburg waterfront, he got even weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far-out corner of Greenpoint.

A dealer with a gallery in Tribeca was the first, but far from the last, to tell me I had to check out Tarlow’s paintings. After an introduction was brokered, Tarlow invited me to lunch at Borgo this past summer. The restaurant has many fantastic pork-laden dishes, but we ate almost entirely vegetables, as well as one very elegant, simple piece of fish. A summer lunch. We fell into an easy patter, talking about exhibitions, other artists—but mostly his painting practice. He’d been working on Long Island, not on the East End but in the middle. He’d had a few shows. There was discussion of representation. He spoke about all this with an unpracticed earnestness and complete confidence. He sounded like a very prominent emerging artist, which, at 56, he is.

“I don’t know if it’s just age or time, or I was too much of a young person, or a young mind, but I’ve been more secure with my ability to hold all these things in the same time,” he told me back in the studio. “I can go work tonight in the restaurant and feel perfectly confident in that work, and I can show you this work and feel perfectly confident in this work. Whereas, I think, as a young person, I felt like, Am I fake?”

Sometimes it’s not the enfant terrible who breaks out—it’s the working parent, the person with a desk job, the successful entrepreneur who back-ends into revolutionary art making. Think William Carlos Williams writing “The Red Wheelbarrow” while working as a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey. Or Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children in San Francisco. Or Jeff Koons working on Wall Street in order to earn money to make his sculptures. Having a demanding job actually granted them the freedom to be artists. Tarlow started drawing during restaurant concept meetings.

Sometimes Tarlow hangs his own paintings upstairs in his brownstone’s salon room, or at his house on Long Island, to see what they look like in the wild. The paintings have a confident thrust to them, with the colors bold-blocked in a way that reminds me of Albert Oehlen, drawing from Roman and Greek mythology in Twombly-esque riffs: visages multiplying and fading like a Kippenberger-ian pomo ride into the ether. Sure, any painter who’s spent time in Europe since the 1990s has wanted to be Martin Kippenberger. But Tarlow has an actual connection to him: Like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a lover of Italian food and good wine, and he made art to hang in restaurants. And like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a restaurant owner, balancing his studio practice with running Capri, a Venice, California, spot in which he invested after moving to Los Angeles in 1989. According to those present at the time, Kippenberger became a part-owner of the place because, as the artist put it, “You can’t get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles.”

As a bartender at The Odeon, Tarlow maintained a working painting studio but found it hard to produce art. After opening Diner, he skipped painting sessions in favor of opening businesses and starting a family. Once that duality settled, he started drawing on the move, carrying sketchbooks and working through potential paintings. Eventually, once the kids got old enough, he built out a studio in a nook of his 19th-century basement.

“I really started painting back downstairs. Let’s just say, after dinner, it was 8 p.m. and they were watching Nemo. No one actually needs me, they’re totally happy. My wife’s up there, everyone’s laughing, giggling with little fish,” he said. “And I can just walk down here and do my thing. Having it in my house for sure is the only way I could do this amount of work, and for sure even get to this place. Because I do think you have to do a certain amount of work to get to this place unless you’re just a born prodigy. But when you think about the genius of Picasso or whomever, he made a million fucking paintings.”

Tarlow didn’t really show anyone his work for a long time.

“I met Andrew socially. I knew his restaurants way before I knew Andrew. And one day he was like, ‘Come and see my studio,’” Tieghi-Walker tells me. “It did not surprise me at all that he had an art studio in his basement and that these were the types of works he was creating.”

The show at Tiwa Select was on view right as Tarlow was getting ready to open Borgo. There was a certain amount of unconscious transference, Tarlow told me. For the Tiwa dinner, instead of creating name placards, the artist hand-sketched an artwork of each guest’s name on the paper tablecloth. Now, when a regular makes a reservation at Borgo, Tarlow will elegantly sketch out their name on the paper tablecloth.

The showcasing of his art at Borgo marks the first time Tarlow has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant. Tarlow doesn’t exactly promote this. When I asked about it, he told me that only one of his own works was up at the moment, then changed the subject. Alex Levy, the media strategist and theater producer, has been a regular at Borgo since it opened. “Borgo is the grown-up Platonic ideal of what a restaurant can be,” he said. After several visits, Levy, who also collects a bit of contemporary art, noticed what was on the walls.

“I complimented one of the paintings, and Andrew said, ‘It’s by my daughter.’ And then he pointed to another one and said, ‘That’s by me,’” Levy says. “I had no idea that there’s this whole other part of him.”

Like Tarlow, Levy balances two seemingly divergent but strangely complementary careers—as a speechwriter on one hand, a Tony Award winner on the other—and Tarlow invited him to see his studio on Long Island. Levy bought a painting immediately. Seeing the studio, Levy says, helped him realize, to some extent, what the special sauce is behind a place like Borgo. It’s for incredibly confident, hyperproductive creative types, run by an artist who has complete faith in his ability to work.

And for Tarlow, the focus and passion in one arena lead right into the passion for the other.

“I’m also being very present for your needs in the same way as I’m trying to be very present with these paintings,” he said. “They’re not separate boats. When the restaurant’s working, I feel creative inside of it.”

#3507. Star Trek's George Takei Played A Villain In A Beloved Batman Series

Throughout its 60-year history, the "Star Trek" franchise has been the home to some truly fantastic voices. The dramatic, over-the-top delivery of William Shatner as Captain Kirk, the sonorous tones of Avery Brooks as Captain Sisko, and the cat-like vocal fry of Kate Mulgrew as Captain Janeway are, in their own way, as iconic as the ships they helmed. You don't need to go all the way to the captain's chair to find those voices, though. George Takei, who played Lieutenant Hikaru Sulu on the original "Trek," had a voice so recognizable that he was able to turn something as simple as "oh my" into a full-on catchphrase.

Needless to say, those signature dulcet tones make him easy to pick out when you hear him showing up somewhere other than the bridge of the USS Enterprise, even when the character he's playing could not look any more different than the man himself. So if you were catching up on one of the best Batman shows ever made, you were not having an audio hallucination. That was in fact George Takei as Mr. Fixx in the two-part pilot of "Batman Beyond."

"Batman Beyond" debuted in 1999 when creators Bruce Timm, Paul Dini, and Alan Burnett came up with a desperate pitch to satisfy the studio's demand for a new Batman show: a slightly sci-fi, near-future take on the Dark Knight. Set decades after the events of "Batman: The Animated Series," the series followed high school student Terry McGinnis (Will Friedle) as he took over the role of Batman from a retired Bruce Wayne, played by legendary "BTAS" voice actor Kevin Conroy. Terry's youth, struggles balancing his Batman identity with life as a cool teen, and wisecracking demeanor gave the character a vibe that was equal parts Batman and Spider-Man. That may have turned off a few viewers at the time who thought a teenage Batman was a ripoff, but the end result speaks for itself.

While he only appeared in the first two episodes, Takei's character was arguably the most important villain in the entire series. Derek Powers, who would go on to become the supervillain Blight, might've been the mastermind who ordered the hit, but it was Mr. Fixx who actually killed Terry's father and set him on the path of vengeance that would lead to him becoming Batman. The casting was an interesting one, too. Fixx had the design of a hulking brute with a scarred eye, but even a few words in Takei's rich voice gave him a depth that subverted looks and hinted at a much deeper character. Unfortunately, that character wound up at the bottom of the ocean off the coast of Gotham City before we could really get into his hopes and dreams, but that's the life of an evil henchman for you.

Takei wasn't the only notable celebrity on "Batman Beyond." Hardcore rocker Henry Rollins had a recurring role as D-list supervillain Mad Stan, former James Bond actor George Lazenby showed up as King, the leader of the Royal Flush Gang, and "Terminator" star Linda Hamilton made an appearance as a scientist who built a new body for a cryogenically preserved Mr. Freeze, among others. Cary Elwes, Tim Curry, Michael McKean, Ice-T ... the list goes on, and it's full of compelling performances that helped to make the show the beloved classic that it is.

If you've got a good ear, "Batman Beyond" is worth watching just for spotting celebrity voices. And if you don't, well, it's worth watching because it's a great take on Batman with some phenomenal episodes and a great design sense. Just don't be surprised if you find yourself thinking some of those supervillains sound awfully familiar.

Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is $74.99 (was $119.99), making it the least expensive option in the lineup for anyone who wants a step up from TV speakers for everyday viewing—it's a 24-inch, two-channel bar that supports DTS Virtual:X and Dolby Audio, though it doesn’t have Dolby Atmos or a separate subwoofer. Despite its name, it's an audio-only soundbar and requires a Fire TV streaming stick for you to get any of the Fire TV experience. For more on this soundbar, read PCMag’s review.

Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is down to $139.99 from $249.99, and the extra money over the base model gets you a dedicated center channel that helps make dialogue easier to follow, along with a built-in subwoofer, Dolby Atmos, and DTS:X support. Amazon Fire TV Soundbar with Alexa Voice Remote Pro is $109.98 (was $154.98). If you don’t specifically want or need the remote, though, the Soundbar Plus is a more capable soundbar for just $30 more.

Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer is $229.99, down from $374.99. This configuration takes the same 3.1-channel bar and pairs it with a separate wireless subwoofer, which gives bass-heavy scenes and film scores considerably more weight than the bar's built-in woofer can manage on its own—and at $90 more than the discounted Soundbar Plus, this is the option I'd consider if fuller bass is a priority. Keep in mind that it doesn't add rear speakers, so you're still working with a 3.1 setup and sound that stays in front of you.

Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer and Surround Sound Speakers is $349.99, down from $489.99. This is the complete 5.1 package, adding two rear speakers to the 3.1 bar and wireless subwoofer, so action scenes and other surround effects come from behind you, rather than only from the direction of the TV—but it costs $120 more than the discounted soundbar and subwoofer bundle, so it’s worth considering how much you want that surround-sound effect. Also, while the rear speakers connect to the soundbar wirelessly, each still needs a power outlet.

#3505. Star Wars' New Jedi Order Era is Officially Moving Forward

Two long-awaited Star Wars movies may still be happening

Despite Star Wars: The Mandalorian & Grogu struggling at the box office, it seems Disney is continuing development on two upcoming Star Wars films. This summer, Star Wars: New Jedi Order and Dave Filoni’s untitled movie as in-development projects were confirmed to be in the works in industry publication Production Weekly, suggesting that despite delays and silence around the projects, they haven't been shelved.

Star Wars: New Jedi Order will reportedly bring back Daisy Ridley as Rey (Skywalker) roughly 15 years after the events of Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker as she rebuilds the Jedi. Considering that the Star Wars fandom has largely negative feelings about the sequel trilogy, especially after The Rise of Skywalker, New Jedi Order’s direct ties to that film will pose a steep challenge.

The project has cycled through several writers. Damon Lindelof (Lost, The Leftovers, Watchmen) and Justin Britt-Gibson were the original screenwriters before Disney fired them — the pair are currently working together on HBO’s superhero detective series, Lanterns. Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight was also set to write, but left the project in 2024. Last January, Variety reported that George Nolfi (The Bourne Ultimatum) is now writing the script. Filmmaker Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy is set to direct the film. New Jedi Order was originally scheduled for release on Dec. 17, 2027, but was removed from Disney’s schedule in May 2025.

Details about Dave Filoni’s untitled film have been scarce, but Production Weekly includes the following description: “The story will focus on the New Republic and will conclude the interconnected narratives told in The Mandalorian, The Book of Boba Fett, Ahsoka, and other Disney Plus series.” While it was previously rumored that the film would tie into recent Disney Plus TV series, it will be interesting to see whether it maintains that premise after The Mandalorian and Grogu underperformed at the box office.

This past January, Filoni took over as president and chief creative officer at Lucasfilm. Filoni has overseen numerous Star Wars TV series, including The Clone Wars, Rebels, Ahsoka, Maul – Shadow Lord, and more. While most of his series have been well received, he’s been criticized for requiring viewers to be familiar with an increasingly complicated and insular TV universe.

The only Star Wars film with a concrete release date is Star Wars: Starfighter, which takes place five years after the events of Rise of Skywalker and stars Ryan Gosling as a pilot. Shawn Levy (Deadpool & Wolverine) is directing the movie. It will be released in theaters on May 28, 2027. While there haven't been many Star Wars films in recent years, the series has stayed active through great TV series like The Ninth Jedi and the recent Star Wars: Zero Company tactics game.

Zero Company has a touch more Andor DNA than you’d expect.

Certainly not mad about seeing Glen Powell in a cowboy hat again.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We've seen Glen Powell chase tornadoes, fly airplanes and play a football player in disguise. Next, he'll be transforming into a country singer for The Comeback King, a comedy he's collaborating with Judd Apatow on that will premiere on the 2027 movie schedule in February. So, what inspired him to put the cowboy hat back on and sing? Well, it turns out Twisters and shotgunning a beer with Luke Combs had something to do with it.

It’s not surprising to hear the Texas native is tapping into his country roots with The Comeback King, but I was surprised to find out the story would follow Powell as Aubrey King, a disgraced famous country singer who must revive his career, and that it was a comedy. After rave reviews for Season 2 of Powell’s Hulu comedy Chad Powers, I’m glad to see him stepping further into the comedic landscape after a string of action films like Top Gun: Maverick, Twisters, and The Running Man. However, I did not expect him to tell Katie and Company that the inspiration behind this new project stemmed from drinking beer with Luke Combs:

I think it was when we were putting together Twisters. We were putting together the Twisters soundtrack that had, you know, Ella [Langley] and Megan Moroney, Bailey Zimmerman, Luke [Combs]. You know, it was like we had a great community, and I was like ‘Man, I just wanna be a part of this world.’ Probably right after I shotgunned beers with Luke Combs on stage. I was like, ‘I need to live here. I wanna do beers for breakfast just like Luke.’

I can’t say I blame the Hit Man actor for getting caught up in that moment with his fellow Twisters castmates and Luke Combs. Together, they all shotgunned beer on stage at Combs’ NYC concert back in the summer of 2024, and the video went viral on TikTok.

As Powell mentions, he got a taste of the country music life putting together the Twisters movie soundtrack, which hit no. 3 on the Billboard country album charts that summer, with Luke Combs’ “Ain’t No Love In Oklahoma” spending 15 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100.

A tale as old as Rocky, if you want a part in a specific film, write it yourself. According to Rolling Stone, Producer Kevin Misher connected Powell with Apatow shortly after the idea for The Comeback King was born, and the Scream Queens actor and the mind behind Knocked Up wrote the script together. This will be Apatow’s first directorial feature film since The Bubble (2022) and The King of Staten Island (2020).

I’m already sold on The Comeback King from the trailer alone. It’s got hilarious roasts, a redemption arc, and a ton of heart, all the hallmarks of a great Judd Apatow film. In The Comeback King, we see Glen Powell live out his wildest “beer for breakfast” fantasies (a nod to Luke Combs “Don’t Tempt Me”), until it all comes crashing down after his pop star girlfriend (Madelyn Cline) cheats and ruins his reputation. King then returns to his old college where his career all started, for redemption and maybe a new shot at love. Check out the trailer below, and see if you can name the insane number of country music cameos:

How Glen Powell was able to once again assemble the Avengers of country music, I’ll never know. But I’m super excited to see the likes of Miranda Lambert, Jelly Roll, Brad Paisley, and Shaboozey bring their A-game alongside Powell in this epic ensemble comedy when it premieres on February 5, 2027. While we wait for that, I think we should all say thank you to Luke Combs too for helping inspire this film that looks like it'll be a lot of country fun.

#3503. Why Magno Stift From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

The "Hunger Games" universe is full of wild, larger-than-life characters, especially when we're talking about denizens of the ultra-wealthy and super-powerful Capitol that controls Panem. Every year, during the annual Hunger Games that cull (or "reap") children from each of Panem's tightly controlled and impoverished 12 districts, Capitol citizens help beautify those kids before sending most of them to their deaths, and many Capitol higher-ups pursue plastic surgery and extreme fashion for high-concept looks.

One of those people in the latest "Hunger Games" book and movie, "Sunrise on the Reaping," is the erratic and unreliable District 12 stylist Magno Stift, who's legally married to the surgically-enhanced District 12 chaperone Drusilla Sickle (an unrecognizable Glenn Close in the film) and who's played on screen by Billy Porter. In the novel, our protagonist Haymitch Abernathy — a young version of the District 12 victor played by Woody Harrelson in the previous "Hunger Games" films and Joseph Zada in this new prequel — notes that nobody speaks highly of Magno, and "he's every bit as bad as they say." He continues, "While the other stylists do new costumes each year for the parade and interviews that happen before the Games, he seems to have a limitless supply of the same crappy coal miner overalls in an array of sizes."

When Magno finally shows up, we see him through Haymitch's eyes: "Magno Stift's sun-leathered skin has been tattooed with a snakeskin pattern. He wears a long shirt made of metal diamonds and no visible pants. His sandals lace all the way up to his pelvis, and from each of his ears dangle tiny, living garter snakes that twist and turn in misery." Eventually, he stops showing up to work when one of his wearable reptiles poisons him. So, why does Magno look familiar in the movie?

You've definitely seen Magno Stift actor Billy Porter in at least one of his recent high-profile projects, so let me walk you through some of them. After earning fame and acclaim for his role as Lola in the Broadway stage musical version of "Kinky Boots," which won him a Tony and a Grammy, Porter's big-screen career slowly began to take off. Though he did, to be totally fair, appear as a singer in the 1996 classic "The First Wives Club," Porter's newfound name recognition in the 2010s earned him roles in films like "The Humbling" alongside Greta Gerwig and Al Pacino, the 2020 comedy "Like a Boss" with Tiffany Haddish, and 2021's "Cinderella," which gave Porter one of his biggest roles yet as the fairy godparent Fab G.

During a 2021 interview with People Magazine, Porter talked about gender-flipping the role played by none other than Whitney Houston in the much-loved 1997 TV film adaptation of the stage musical "Rodgers & Hammerstein's Cinderella" starring Brandy. "When I was 14, my dream was to be the male Whitney Houston," the actor quipped before adding, ""Magic has no gender. That is the most important for me."

After starring in "Cinderella" with Camilla Cabello and James Corden, Porter directed the coming-of-age film "Anything's Possible," popped up in the senior comedy "80 for Brady," and got dramatic in "Our Son" with Luke Evans and Andrew Rannells. So, what about Porter's small-screen career? It's booming, too.

Billy Porter's early years on TV include credits on "So You Think You Can Dance" as a performer and stalwart procedurals like "Law & Order," as well as its massively successful spin-off "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" — but after winning that Tony and Emmy and hosting an eight-episode 2013 special called "Land of Lola: Backstage at Kinky Boots," Porter was finally on the map. Aside from "American Horror Story: Apocalypse" and other recurring and guest arcs on shows like the 2021 "Gossip Girl" reboot, Porter's most recognizable role is as Prayerful "Pray" Tell, an emcee in the New York ballroom scene, on Ryan Murphy's series "Pose." Not only did Porter get the chance to play a character who shares his HIV diagnosis (something the actor revealed in his own life in 2021), he won an Emmy for playing Pray Tell and became the first-ever gay Black man to win in any lead Emmy category. As Porter told People Magazine in 2021, it was also an important role for him for other reasons:

"'Pose' and Pray Tell have been a proxy for my healing. The trauma was so difficult. The grief was so heavy. The antiretroviral drugs [for HIV] came, and everybody moved on. There's a whole generation of us that really never got a chance to process having lived through the AIDS crisis [and] having lived through an epidemic."

You can see Billy Porter (briefly) play Magno Stift in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," which is currently playing in theaters.

#3502. Google Killed Its Dark Web Report, but You Can Still Monitor Data Breaches

Google’s Dark Web Report used to be the only consumer-focused platform that let users scan major data breaches, dark web marketplaces, and private forums to see if their personal information had ended up in the hands of hackers. But the company discontinued the service at the start of 2026, with new scans stopping on Jan. 15 and all accounts deleted on Feb. 16.

Google says it sunsetted Dark Web Report because, although the information it provided was generally useful, the service failed to provide “helpful next steps” for users whose data was found on the dark web. Google promised a new service that would provide more actionable intel, but that service has yet to materialize, and there haven’t been any further announcements about it yet.

Dark Web Report may not have been perfect, but it was the only early warning system of its kind that was available for personal use and let users run scans free of cost. Now that it’s gone, however, there are plenty of other services that offer the same service at varying costs and levels of effectiveness. Let’s talk through the nature of the insight that Google's reports offered, how it collected that information in the first place, and what options exist in the market to replace it.

Google launched the Dark Web Report in March 2023 as a premium feature available to Google One users, but later extended it for free to anyone with a Google account and moved it to the "Results about you" dashboard.

You'd set up a monitoring profile with your name, date of birth, physical address, phone number, emails, and Social Security Number if you lived in the U.S. After that, you could head to the dashboard anytime you wanted to run a free scan across dark web forums and marketplaces, publicly disclosed corporate data breaches, and other hidden online spaces to see if any of your personal information had shown up there. It was easy to use—but not a lot of people knew it existed in the first place.

It’s unclear what prompted the internal decision at Google, but in the absence of concrete next steps, it is reasonable to think the reports could create panic for the uninitiated. There’s no way to remove your information from the dark web once it’s already in circulation there. Still, having an early warning so you could reset 2FA or self-lock your SSN isn’t without merit.

But perhaps more importantly, most people with Google accounts didn’t know and hadn’t heard of the Dark Web Report’s existence. Google has likely taken it as a hint that users want more active remediation tools than simple alerts, which is why it’s now directing users to the Password Manager, Passkeys, and “Results about you” dashboard instead—though, again, the company hasn't followed through on a direct replacement for Dark Web Report, despite teasing such a feature.

Many of the top dark web scanners draw from the same well of information, scanning against major data breaches and dark web spaces. Several also offer breach notifications that send you email alerts when your details show up in a periodic scan. However, none of that is worth paying for because Have I Been Pwned or Mozilla Monitor cover those features quite well for free. Even the default password managers from Google and Apple come with some ability to monitor leaked credentials.

There isn’t an easy way to scrub your information from the dark web once it ends up getting leaked. But you can take steps to protect sensitive information or financial data once you know there’s been a leak. If a password has been compromised, reset it immediately. Also, enable 2FA on the affected account for added security. Even better, switch to a passkey if that account supports it. If not, authenticator apps are a safer way to receive 2FA codes than standard SMS.

If your Social Security number has been leaked, freeze your credit with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You can do this by contacting each agency separately. Freezing your credit will prevent unauthorized credit withdrawals and protect your credit score from abuse by attackers. If one of your credit or debit card numbers has ended up in a breach, call your bank to freeze transactions on that card immediately.

Finally, get in the habit of using email aliases instead of sharing your actual email address with every platform and service provider. Addy.io and Proton’s SimpleLogin are both popular services that let you generate temporary email aliases that point to your inbox.

#3501. Sotheby’s Sold the World’s Most Expensive Van Gogh for $190 Million

This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors, from New York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

One thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in New York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

Speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.

We’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this issue: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian

Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

So who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of New York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is currently on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

The $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

— As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

The 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

— Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

— The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred said the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”

— For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

— Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. The evening raised $1.5 million for Ballroom Marfa.

— After the auction on Wednesday, the gallery Entrance, a space opened by dealer Louis Shannon on Ludlow Street nearly a decade ago, hosted an opening for the painter Victoire Bourgois. Lots of artists were there to support her—Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin—and the event was followed by a dinner at the ultimate Dimes Square redoubt. That’s right: Dimes itself. Can you believe Dimes has been open for—checks age—more than 13 years? And guess what? After all the Dimes Square discourse, the actual restaurant itself still slaps.

— The annual Baby2Baby Gala went down in LA last weekend. I wasn’t able to make it out West, but luckily for Vanity Fair, Tallulah Willis was on the scene and wrote a fabulous party report that you can read here. I also want to note that the live auction of artworks, curated, as always, by Darrow Contemporary founder Meredith Darrow, included an Annie Morris sculpture that achieved $410,000.

On a Friday in November, I walk into Gagosian on Madison Avenue for a meeting with Michael Chow, the artist, collector, filmmaker, designer, actor, and founder of the restaurant Mr. Chow. There’s a portrait of Chow by Jean-Michel Basquiat, a portrait by Julian Schnabel, a portrait by Andy Warhol. There’s a drawing of Chow by David Hockney, made soon after Mr. Chow opened in London in 1968.

Michael Chow: So I opened that restaurant. You’ve got Hockney, you’ve got fashion, you’ve got every single thing. It’s almost like a Dada movement on the First World War thing. This one is in London—all happening.

He starts talking about duopolys: Christie’s versus Sotheby’s, Coke versus Pepsi. There was an Italian restaurant in London’s Soho, so he opened a Chinese restaurant in Soho with Italian waiters. He has a theory about name-dropping.

Chow: I hate people who drop names, and Lady Gaga agrees with me.

Why is name-dropping important? Because the minute I say “Napoleon,” you will go there immediately. So it saves a lot of time. Okay, so why am I saying that? Do you know who Robert Fraser is?

The art dealer from the ’60s. Groovy Bob.

I was looking forward to meeting him, blah, blah, blah. He was sitting there. Name-dropping. Sitting in front is Jim Dine. Name-dropping again. I say, “I would like to borrow some paintings.” I said, “Just like”—do you know the Kronenhalle restaurant?

We walk over to the Hockney portrait of Michael Chow sitting in his restaurant.

Chow: The first person I went to is David. He drew one and I said, “Boy.” You know what he did? Tore it all up.

Simultaneously, I went to Peter Blake. I say, “Give me a painting that’s the antithesis of racism,” which he did. At that time he’s into the circus, he’s into all that shit. All right? So I asked him, “Why did you do that?” He did a portrait. So now Peter Blake is fucking crazy. He loves the circus, he loves wrestling and all that shit.

Larry Gagosian walks in and gives Chow a fist bump. Gagosian takes a long look at the Schnabel and then flips through a book of drawings made by artists for 57th Street’s Mr. Chow when it was the art world’s clubhouse. We walk up to the Basquiat.

True Colors: To have it as this sort of landscape, you have the horizon line here, but it’s almost like a Western. It’s almost cinematic.

Shane. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. High Noon.

I’m going to act out the first scene of each. Okay, High Noon.

He uses his hand to pull a finger gun on me, then gets distracted by the Ed Ruscha and the Warhol double portrait.

Chow: Andy said, “Oh, what do you want?” I said, “Hold the color and add lots of diamonds.”

Gagosian brings up Anselm Kiefer, and then Richard Serra.

Chow: If you look at the year 2000, Charlie Rose and Richard Serra, their conversation on the culture of China, and Richard Serra identifies very clearly what is fine art: poetry, music, sculpture, and painting.

The works in the show are for sale. I ask Chow if he’s emotional about parting with them. He seems very calm.

Chow: I’m only a temporary steward of the works.

“Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow” is up at Gagosian’s 980 Madison space until December 22.

#3500. New Dungeons & Dragons Live-Action Series Officially Replaces Netflix's Forgotten Realms

The Mists are apparently rolling into Netflix.

A live-action Dungeons & Dragons series based on Ravenloft is in development at Netflix, giving the tabletop gaming franchise’s most famous horror setting its own shot at TV. The project, simply titled Ravenloft, comes from screenwriter John August, Alfonso Cuarón, and Hasbro Entertainment, and is described as the successor to Netflix's other, now-canceled D&D project, The Forgotten Realms.

While Dungeons & Dragons is often associated with taverns, dragons, treasure, and quippy adventuring parties, Ravenloft is the game’s gothic nightmare corner. It’s the place where D&D trades high-fantasy heroics for haunted castles, cursed lands, tragic monsters and the sense that there's always something lurking in the fog.

Ravenloft has been one of D&D’s most iconic settings for decades, dating back to the original 1983 adventure built around Count Strahd von Zarovich. Strahd remains the setting’s defining villain — he's a vampire lord, tragic monster, and tyrant trapped in the mist-shrouded land of Barovia.

The setting later grew into the Domains of Dread, a collection of horror realms ruled by Darklords who are often imprisoned in worlds shaped by their own sins and obsessions. The premise gives the TV show a lot of flexibility in the stories it tells, bouncing between gothic horrors, cursed folklore, and actual nightmares within the one setting.

That flexibility is a big part of why Ravenloft has endured. While Curse of Strahd remains the best-known modern entry point for many D&D players, newer books like Van Richten’s Guide to Ravenloft and Ravenloft: The Horrors Within have expanded the setting beyond Barovia, turning it into a toolkit for nearly every flavor of horror D&D can support.

According to a Deadline report, the Ravenloft project is also part of a broader push to expand D&D outside the core tabletop game. Netflix had also been developing The Forgotten Realms, though Deadline reports Ravenloft is now positioned as its successor. Meanwhile, a sequel to Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves remains uncertain, even though co-writer and co-director Jonathan Goldstein recently said a script exists.

D&D’s reach has also been boosted by projects that don’t look like traditional tabletop products. People are still playing, modding and arguing about Baldur’s Gate 3 years after its 2023 launch, while Critical Role has helped turn actual play into a major entertainment lane of its own, with live shows, animated adaptations, and a huge audience beyond the table.

Ravenloft: The Horrors Within is a good update of Van Richten's Guide to Ravenloft, despite some typical 5.5e design choices
