#3472. 58 Years Later, Captain Kirk's Best Star Trek Quote Is the Greatest Line in Sci-Fi History

This Captain Kirk speech says more about what Star Trek stands for than any other line in the original series.

Some lines of dialogue become so famous they stop belonging to the movies and TV shows that produced them. “May the Force be with you.” “I’ll be back.” “You're gonna need a bigger boat.” You don't need to know the context. The words have long since transcended their original context and permeated the pop culture zeitgeist.

Star Trek: The Original Series has plenty of those. Spock’s wish that everyone to “Live long and prosper” is arguably the franchise's signature phrase. He also turned the simple word “fascinating” into a catchphrase simply by raising one eyebrow before saying it. Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley) spent three seasons reminding everyone, “I'm a doctor, not a…” and, at least in our collective memory declaring, “He's dead, Jim” while standing over the latest redshirt who wandered a little too far from the landing party.

But if I could only pick one line to represent everything Star Trek stands for, it would be four simple words spoken by Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner) halfway through “Return to Tomorrow," the 20th episode of season 2:

On the surface, it doesn't seem like an obvious choice. It's not printed on T-shirts nearly as often as “live long and prosper.” It isn't endlessly quoted by people who have never watched an episode of Star Trek. And unlike “beam me up, Scotty,” it never became part of the broader pop culture vocabulary. But that's exactly why it's the best quote. It doesn't just capture Kirk. It captures the entire philosophy of Star Trek.

First broadcast on Feb. 9, 1968, the episode “Return to Tomorrow” finds the Enterprise answering a mysterious distress call from a dead planet. There, Kirk and his crew discover Sargon, one of three survivors of an ancient civilization that has existed as beings of pure energy for half a million years. Sargon asks Kirk, Spock (Leonard Nimoy), and Dr. Ann Mulhall (Diana Muldaur) to temporarily surrender their bodies so he, his wife Thalassa, and the ambitious Henoch can build android bodies and begin life again. Dr. McCoy believes the aliens are manipulating them. Kirk believes the chance to learn from a civilization hundreds of thousands of years more advanced than humanity is worth the danger.

The episode also marks the first of three Star Trek appearances by Diana Muldaur. She plays Dr. Ann Mulhall here before returning as Miranda Jones in the third season episode “Is There in Truth No Beauty?” Years later, she'd become a series regular on Star Trek: The Next Generation as Dr. Katherine Pulaski. “Return to Tomorrow” is also a fun piece of Trek trivia because it's one of the times Spock describes Sargon as “pure energy,” a phrase longtime fans immediately recognize.

Faced with allowing unimaginably powerful aliens to occupy the bodies of his crew, Kirk doesn't issue an order. He makes an argument and reminds his crew that every leap forward in human history required someone willing to embrace uncertainty.

"They used to say if man could fly, he'd have wings," Kirk says. "But he did fly. He discovered he had to." He likens Sargon's offer to humanity's own journey from the Moon to Mars and eventually the stars, arguing that the potential for knowledge outweighs the danger. Only then does he arrive at the four words that define both the captain and the franchise. Those four words explain Kirk better than decades of pop-culture impressions ever could.

For years, pop culture has reduced Kirk to an oversimplified caricature: the swaggering captain who punches first, flirts with every alien woman he meets, and somehow loses his shirt during every other away mission. The real Kirk is far more thoughtful than that. He takes risks, certainly, but not because he enjoys gambling. He takes them because he believes some opportunities are too important to ignore.

There's a world of difference between being reckless and accepting risk in pursuit of discovery. Kirk isn't arguing that danger is exciting. He's arguing that progress is impossible without it.

More importantly, he's explaining what separates Starfleet from almost every other organization. Plenty of fictional explorers travel because they're ordered to. Others do it for conquest, profit, or survival. Starfleet goes because knowledge itself is worth pursuing.

That's why I think this quote is even more meaningful than the famous opening narration about boldly going where no one has gone before. The opening tells us what the Enterprise does. This one explains why.

The timing of the episode makes the speech even more remarkable. “Return to Tomorrow” aired in early 1968, roughly 17 months before Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. America was still trying to prove humans could successfully reach another world, and Star Trek was already imagining the next step beyond that. Kirk's speech places the Enterprise in the same lineage as every explorer who came before it, suggesting humanity's future won't be built by playing it safe.

That idea has become the beating heart of Star Trek. Optimism, in the Star Trek universe, has never meant believing everything will work out. It means believing the unknown is worth facing anyway.

There are more famous quotes in The Original Series. There are funnier ones. There are certainly more quotable ones. But no other line distills what Star Trek has always been trying to say better than four words Kirk spoke nearly 60 years ago: “Risk is our business.”

#3471. Why Beetee Latier From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping."

Prequel film "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" reveals the details of how Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada, Woody Harrelson in the original films) won the 50th Hunger Games ... and lost everything else in his life, turning him into a miserable man using alcohol to cope. Yet "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" revealed Haymitch wasn't merely the burnout he first appeared to be, but a key member of the rebellion against the Capitol.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" shows the beginning of that, particularly Haymitch's early alliance with Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons, filling in for the late Philip Seymour Hoffman). Younger versions of several past Hunger Games victors first introduced in "Catching Fire" also show up in "Sunrise on the Reaping," including the tech wizard Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr. doing an uncanny vocal impression of original Beetee actor Jeffrey Wright).

Beetee has already been caught rebelling against the Capitol. As punishment, his own son Ampert (Percy Daggs IV) was reaped into the Hunger Games. Beetee and Haymitch collaborate as part of a conspiracy to have Haymitch disrupt the arena's mechanical systems and, hopefully, sabotage the Games once he's inside. When Haymitch does so, but the Games persist and, when the conspiracy is discovered, he takes the fall. The Capitol has already done the worst thing it could to Beetee by taking his son, and as a victor, he's too valuable and visible a symbol to kill.

"Hunger Games" fans already know this isn't the last we've seen of Beetee, and this probably isn't the first you've seen of his actor who plays him. Born in New Orleans in 1994, Harrison is the son of two musicians, but he chose acting as his primary creative path.

Harrison's film career began with incidental parts in "12 Years A Slave" and "Ender's Game" in 2013, which were followed by his first starring role in 2017's post-apocalyptic horror film "It Comes At Night." Harrison played the character of Travis, son of Paul (Joel Edgerton) and Sarah (Carmen Ejogo).

In 2018, Harrison appeared in "Monster," Netflix's adaptation of Walter Dean Myers's 1999 novel about a Black honor student accused of murder. The following year, Harrison starred in a surprisingly similar film: the psychodrama "Luce," playing a former child soldier from Eritrea adopted by a wealthy white couple (Naomi Watts and Tim Roth). Luce is a straight-A student, popular athlete, and seemingly on his way to great things ... until he writes an essay that appears to defend radical political violence as a valid means of change.

Having proved himself with those leading roles, Harrison has continued making himself into one of Hollywood's most prolific young actors even before joining "The Hunger Games." Several of his prominent roles have been in historical dramas: In 2021, he played Black Panther leader Fred Hampton in 2021's "The Trial of the Chicago 7," and in 2022's "Elvis" he played Blues musician B.B. King. Harrison also played Martin Luther King Jr. in Season 4 of National Geographic series "Genius," opposite Aaron Pierre (now known as John Stewart from "Lanterns") as Malcolm X.

But that's not all Harrison can do. He played Christian de Neuvillette in Joe Wright's 2021 musical film "Cyrano," adapting the 1897 French play by Edmond Rostand. In 2024 "Lion King" prequel "Mufasa," he voiced Scar. Being in company with Jeremy Irons and Chiwetel Ejiofor is pretty impressive for an actor Harrison's age.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is now in theaters.

#3470. The iPhone Duo Is Getting Face Unlock

Apple dropped iOS 27.2.1 last week, patching a handful of security vulnerabilities and bugs—including two iMessage flaws that let people read messages they shouldn't. But while most of us are running this version (or should install it as soon as possible), others are running something different—iOS 27.3.

Apple is currently beta testing the third major update in the iOS 27 era, and anyone—developer and public tester alike—is free to install it at their leisure. With it, comes the return of the Health app, vertical Safari tabs, and Siri AI app actions, among other new features. But for users of Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 brings two rather notable changes—both of which are for the better.

With the second iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple is introducing face unlock for the iPhone Duo. The foldable famously ships with Touch ID, the first new iPhone since the third-gen iPhone SE to do so. While that isn't a problem per se, many of us are used to unlocking our iPhones with our faces. This update just lets new Duo owners keep up with that muscle memory.

Now, take note: This isn't Face ID. No software update can introduce new hardware, so the iPhone Duo still doesn't have the camera tech required to power Apple's Face ID system. As such, the Duo's face unlock is likely not as secure as Face ID on other iPhones. Perhaps that's why your iPhone Duo will require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. This feature seems to be one of pure convenience: If you want to be able to unlock your Duo with your face (at least, some of the time), you can.

What's more, this isn't a default setting. If you're running the beta, or if you're reading this after iOS 27.3 drops, you can find the option in Settings > Touch ID & Passcode.

Apple made a big deal about the continuity involved with opening and closing the iPhone Duo. As you do, your content moves with you seamlessly—a very Apple thing to do. That said, you might expect folding the Duo to lock it, but it doesn't. You need to hit the side button to actually put the phone to sleep.

iOS 27.3 changes that. If you so choose, you can enable a setting to lock your Duo whenever you close it. That won't work for everyone, of course—some users may still want to move between modes without worrying about locking their Duos. But for those who would rather lock their devices whenever they fold them up, the new option is under Settings > Display & Brightness.

#3469. Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’

In 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived). On Wednesday night, Hill spoke before a packed screening at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and looked back on the movie that jump-started not only his screenwriting endeavors, but a directing career that would ultimately include classics like “The Warriors,” “48hrs.,” and “Streets of Fire.” Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

“The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts. “The Getaway” was, appropriately enough, selected by the writers branch, and screenwriter and Academy Governor Larry Karaszewski was on hand to introduce the movie and moderate the pre-screening discussion with Hill. Karaszewski, a longtime “Getaway” enthusiast who carried newspaper ads from the movie around in his wallet when he was 10 years old, pointed out that Hill changed the entire architecture of screenwriting when he burst onto the scene in the early 1970s.

“ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski said. “We have an award show here at the Oscars called the Sci-Tech Awards, where they give awards to things that silently change the industry and advance them into the future. I really feel that Walter Hill did that in screenwriting, but it wasn’t a technical advancement. It was a literary advancement. He changed what a page should look like as a screenplay and what it could feel like to read it.” Karaszewski went on to illustrate his point by projecting pages from Robert Bolt’s “Doctor Zhivago” screenplay and Walter Hill’s “Hard Times” side by side on the screen.

“You don’t even have to read [Bolt’s script], just look at it,” Karaszewski said, pointing out the dense blocks of words compared to Hill’s lean, spare page. “You’re looking at monoliths. It’s dense, and there are camera moves and references to things you would never see on screen. Walter Hill taught screenwriters that you can strip all that away. You can still direct on the page, but not by calling for specific camera movements — just by saying what you’re seeing. Walter’s scripts are made out of short sentences and white space. He looked at the placement of each line as part of the storytelling. He turned the carriage return into an art form.”

As Karaszewski welcomed Hill to the stage, he pointed out that “The Getaway” — a smart, terse tale of a couple (Steve McQueen and Ali MacGraw) on the run after their involvement in a botched bank robbery — represented the emergence of Hill’s developing voice. “You’ll already see the beginnings of that remarkable style, the economy, the precision, the sense that every line is pushing you toward the next image.” Yet, as Hill revealed in his lively conversation with Karaszewski, the ruthless efficiency of the pacing and the concentrated emotional impact of “The Getaway” were not easily arrived at.

“I think it’s much harder to adapt than it is to write an original, which is the reverse of the normal theory,” Hill said. “With an original, it’s just you at your desk with the typewriter or pen. When you’re adapting, that almost always means that somebody else owns it, so you’re not simply writing based on your own opinions about what should be in and what should be out, but there’s the producer’s opinion, and the studio’s, and the actor’s. There were all these political currents that one had to navigate.”

One such political current came from megastar McQueen, who didn’t interfere much with Hill’s writing but did have one caveat that amused the screenwriter. “He wanted to play a reasonably sympathetic outlaw,” Hill said. “That was not in the Thompson sensibility. So we already had a disparity, but the producer wanted to keep Steve happy.”

“The Getaway” began as an assignment not for Peckinpah, but for Peter Bogdanovich, who was white-hot coming off of successes like “The Last Picture Show” and “What’s Up, Doc?” Bogdanovich didn’t last long, however, given his clashes with McQueen and McQueen’s power as the film‘s star. “I couldn’t imagine two more diverse sensibilities than Steve and Peter,” Hill said, noting that he had his own disagreements with Bogdanovich over the movie’s tone but wasn’t in a position to argue. “You’ve got to remember, I was nobody. I had one screen credit. And these were big players.”

The big players included not only Bogdanovich and McQueen, but MacGraw, hot off of the smash hit “Love Story.” MacGraw was pushed into the movie by her husband, Paramount studio chief Robert Evans, which Hill found amusing given the way everything played out. “I’m going to tread lightly here,” Hill said of the behind-the-scenes melodrama involving MacGraw leaving Evans when she fell in love with McQueen. “When the material was optioned and I was hired, Bob saw the movie as a fabulous idea for Steve and Ali. It didn’t work out so well for him.”

After Bogdanovich and McQueen butted heads, Bogdanovich was let go and Peckinpah, who McQueen had enjoyed working with on “Junior Bonner,” came in to take his place. “We were very lucky to get such a talented guy, obviously,” Hill said. “I thought of him then and I think of him now as one of the great directors with a very unique sensibility. I was very privileged to work with him — which doesn’t mean he and I agreed about everything.”

Hill’s biggest disagreement with Peckinpah had to do with a scene in which MacGraw’s character considered killing McQueen before turning the gun on his nemesis — and the man with whom MacGraw had gone to bed to secure McQueen’s early release from prison. This was a scene carried over from the book, which was darker and more paranoid than what made it to the screen given McQueen’s mandate that he be sympathetic. Hill felt that the moment no longer worked now that the relationship between McQueen and MacGraw was softer and more relatable in the novel.

“I thought that for the movie we were trying to make, you might forgive your wife for sleeping with a bad man to do a very good thing for you,” Hill said. “That seemed to be to be conceivable. But if your wife fell into cahoots with the bad guy and actually was thinking about killing you and actually turned the gun on you before she decided to shoot the other guy…this did not track for me. But this is the screenwriter’s dilemma: you either talk the director into your point of view, or you make the change that he wants — or somebody else will. Those are your choices.”

Hill lost the argument but liked the movie Peckinpah made in the end. “He staged it beautifully,” Hill said. “He shot it beautifully. It’s got one of Steve’s best performances. And the movie turned out to be his greatest hit. He used to call me every once in a while after I became a director and say, ‘Write me another one.'” Ironically, it was the success of “The Getaway” that put Hill in a position where didn’t have to write for other directors anymore.

“Larry Gordon had a producing deal to make low-budget movies at Columbia,” Hill said. “He would give young writers a chance to direct, because he said, ‘Even if they’re no good as directors, at least we’ll get a good script. Most of the directors I’m working with aren’t any good anyway.'” Gordon gave Hill the opportunity to direct “Hard Times,” and the rest was history. Aside from kicking off Hill’s directing career, the collaboration became the first of many between the two men. “He’s a wonderful guy and a wonderful producer.”

Now in his 80s, Hill continues to write and direct (his last film was the exquisite character-driven Western “Dead for a Dollar“), plying his trade in the world of graphic novels in between film projects. “I’ve had four of them published in France,” Hill said, joking that the only one published in America was “the least good of them,” but promising another one on the way. “You’ve got to keep your hand in somehow.”

For information on Academy Museum programs, visit their website.

#3468. Before Spider-Man, Kirsten Dunst Was In An Episode Of Star Trek: The Next Generation

If you're the kind of person who has fun spotting celebrities in roles they took before they were launched to the heights of their fame, you could do a lot worse than throwing on a few episodes of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and keeping your eye out for guest stars. Before he starred in "The Rocketeer" and took on the infamous Transylvanian count in "Bram Stoker's Dracula," Billy Campbell played the roguish Okona in "TNG's" second season, and before she had her breakout role in "Double Jeopardy" opposite Tommy Lee Jones, Ashley Judd made her acting debut in Season 5, playing an ensign in the episode where the crew of the Enterprise were all taken over by an evil video game.

These early appearances are always fun to catch, especially when the actor you're spotting is both immediately recognizable and just about to break out heights so high that you'd almost need a starship to catch up to them. The best example? Kirsten Dunst, who made an appearance in the final season of "The Next Generation," long before she'd star as Mary Jane Watson in Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" films.

On the Season 7 episode "Dark Page", an 11-year-old Dunst played Hedril, a member of the Cairn, a species of alien telepaths who, as Captain Picard puts it, "have no concept of spoken language." To help facilitate communication, the Federation sends in their own telepath, occasional ambassador and perpetual thorn in Picard's side Lwaxana Troi (Majel Barrett), the mother of the Enterprise's empathic counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis).

Unfortunately, the Cairn's first attempt at connecting with an alien species goes awry, and Hedril winds up triggering Lwaxana's repressed memories of Deanna's older sister Kestra, who died when Deanna was a baby.

As a result, Dunst plays both Hedril and, in scenes where Deanna has to explore her mom's mindscape to find out while she's in a coma, a version of Kestra — who, it should be noted, had never been seen or mentioned before on the series, and was even unknown to Deanna.

The episode aired in 1993, and while it wasn't Dunst's first role as a child actress, it was the most prominent by far at the time. Of course, that would all change the following year with the release of "Interview With the Vampire," in which Dunst had her true breakout role playing the vampire Claudia, alongside Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt. Despite Pitt's difficulties in filming that led him to start feeling like an actual vampire, the movie was a financial and critical success, and Dunst in particular earned praise from Roger Ebert for the role and an MTV Movie Award for Best Supporting Actress and a Golden Globe nomination.

Dunst would go on to bigger fame as the star of the iconic cheerleading comedy "Bring It On" and, of course, the romantic lead of Sam Raimi's "Spider-Man" trilogy. As for Hedril, she was one of many one-off characters who never returned to the Enterprise, but Kestra had a bit more of an interesting legacy. A novel set in an alternate universe called "Q and A" cast her, and not Deanna, as the counselor of the Enterprise, and in the first season of "Star Trek: Picard," it was revealed that Deanna would go on to name her own daughter Kestra in a tribute to her dearly departed sister.

#3467. The Best Early Tech Deals From Walmart’s 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sale

During WWDC 26 earlier this summer, Apple announced new Siri AI upgrades with watchOS 27—but only some Apple Watches have compatibility. It's a great option for anyone looking to get into Garmin for the first time or upgrading from anything below it.

Bone conduction headphones are ideal for activities where it is vital to be able to hear your surroundings. At the high end of Shokz's offerings sit the OpenRun Pro 2, which impressed me when I tested them out for review. Walmart currently has a restored pair for $95 (originally $135.95 and $179.99 new).

They're $179 on Walmart as an early Black Friday deal, down from $249 and matching their lowest price ever.

Compare a soundbar's size to the thin, small speakers jammed into modern TVs. The Vizio 4.1 Pro Soundbar and rear speakers come with Dolby Atmos support and cost just $79 (originally $148). They won't win any audio awards, but it's better than any built-in TV speakers, and for $79, it'll improve your experience without breaking the bank.

If you want to take things up a notch, consider this 5.1 channel sound system. Not only does it include far more channels than a single soundbar, but you're also adding a dedicated subwoofer to the mix. A subwoofer will make those thuds, explosions, and low vibrations much more pronounced than on a soundbar alone. For $149.99 (originally $249.99), you can get the ULTIMEA 5.1 surround sound system, which comes with a soundbar—replicating left, right, and center channels—two rear speakers, and a subwoofer.

I love projectors and Roku. To me, a Roku projector just makes sense, especially at $119.99 (originally $389.99). This projector is portable and has the Roku OS already installed, so it's easy to project it against a wall, ceiling, or screen, whether it's indoors or outdoors. It's easy to set up; you just need an outlet nearby and to dim or turn off the lights. If you have Bluetooth speakers, you can hook them up to create a more immersive sound.

The TCL Q51GB is a QLED Google TV that is a great value for anyone looking for size, color, and features. The 98-inch class is heavily discounted at its $898 price (originally $1,499.99). This TV supports Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, and if you're a gamer, you get a refresh rate of 240Hz that is automatically triggered with its Auto Game Mode feature.

The Oura Ring 5 holds the title of the "world's smallest smart ring", with a focus on a slim design and lightweight barely-there feel.

After wearing the Oura Ring 5 for five months, I must say that it lives up to its title. Not once have I ever felt any discomfort from wearing the ring, with its sleep design never interfering with my sleep. Thanks to the sizing kit, it fits like a glove, too.

The Oura Ring 5's fit was a breath of fresh air compared to the Apple Watch Ultra that I wore to bed for a few months before I obtained the Oura Ring 5. Granted, the Apple Watch Ultra is a lot bigger and bulkier than the newer Apple Watch models, such as the Apple Watch 12.

But all Apple Watches are exactly that: watches. I find any wristwatch uncomfortable to wear in bed, particularly smartwatches with heavy screens and tight straps (you need plenty of skin contact for tracking accuracy). But that's a personal preference and if you don't mind something bulky on your wrist in bed, you might sleep happily in the Apple Watch 12.

As for the Garmin, the lead tester in our Garmin Index Sleep Monitor review found the armband design to be surprisingly comfortable and lightweight. The band is available in two sizes (S-M and L-XL), and its screen-free design means it isn't weighed down by heavy monitors.

When it comes down to it, the Oura, Apple, and Garmin sleep trackers share a lot of core sleep tracking features. For example, not only do all three tell you how long you slept, but also how much of that sleep duration was spent in deep sleep, REM sleep, and core sleep (along with how long your night-time awakenings last). They also all provide sleep scores, which measure your overall sleep quality on a scale of 1 to 100.

You can find the key sleep metrics in the Oura app, Garmin Connect app, and the Apple Health app respectively. For the screenless Oura and Garmin, this is the only way to view your sleep data. But you get immediate feedback from your Apple Watch via the Vitals app on the monitor.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide more sleep tracking accuracy than the Oura Ring 4, with a build that improves the sensors' contact with skin and 12% more accuracy in its overnight Heart Rate Variability (HRV) monitoring.

I've found the Oura Ring one of the most dependable consumer sleep trackers on the market. It's especially good at knowing when you're asleep vs awake; studies show up to 96% accuracy when compared to clinical polysomnography (PSG).

I can see the Oura Ring 5's accuracy first hand. When I wore the Oura Ring 5 and the Apple Watch (Ultra) at the same time, I felt the Oura Ring's data reflected how I felt in the morning more accurately than the Apple Watch. For instance, my Apple Watch sleep scores are always much higher than my Oura Ring — despite regularly getting under seven hours of sleep.

That said, the Apple Watch does provide a sleep apnea detection tool (available on the Apple Watch Series 10 and up), which analyzes your breathing patterns to detect disturbances that might signal sleep apnea.

Meanwhile, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor provides a readiness score, which tells you how prepared your body is to handle daily activities (such as workouts) based on your sleep data.

Our lead tester for the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor, Eve Davies, said that the Garmin is "more focused on overnight breathing rates, oxygen levels and respiration rates — is essentially more ‘nerdy’ and geared towards athletic recovery". For data lovers, there's a lot to unpack.

It's also worth mentioning that the Oura Ring 5's sleep latency metric is missing from the Apple Watch and Index Sleep Monitor. And its unique circadian scoring, which uses sleep data over time to identify your sleep chronotype, can help you identify how well your sleep routine aligns with your circadian rhythm.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide around six to nine days of battery life on a single charge. A full charge (from zero to 100) is said to take up to 80 minutes, though I find it charges much faster than this.

That said, I've never found that my ring's battery life has lasted nine days (or even a full week), but this may be due to the fact that I wear a size 7 — the smaller sizes have a shorter battery life.

However, the lifespan of an Oura Ring is that of a giant tortoise when compared with the Apple Watch. The Apple Watch requires daily charging, with the latest 12th Generation's battery life lasting no longer than 24 hours.

The Garmin has quite a lengthy battery life, lasting up to eight nights (however, this can depend on your sleep duration). However, you also wear it less than the Oura Ring 5 or Apple Watch — if you strapped it to yourself all day, expect that battery life to go right down.

✅ You want in-depth sleep tracking: The Oura Ring 5's accuracy is renowned, while its unique sleep features (such as its Body Clock feature) sets it apart.

✅ You value optimal sleep comfort: Thanks to a custom fit and a sleek, lightweight build, the Oura Ring 5 is perfect for a barely-there feel.

✅ You don't own an iPhone: You need an iPhone to set up your Apple Watch, so consider the Oura Ring 5 if you're an Android user.

✅ You don't want to pay monthly fees: The Apple Watch has no hidden subscription costs.

✅ You want immediate feedback: With a screen to view your metrics, the Apple Watch is the only option that doesn't require fiddling about with an app.

✅ You want more versatility: There's a lot more to the Apple Watch than sleep tracking, including highly-rated fitness tracking, and there are plenty of models to suit your requirements.

✅ You want the most budget-friendly tracker: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is never sold over $170, and you can reliably find it on sale during holiday seasons.

✅ You just want a sleep tracker: While the Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch put a lot of energy into fitness and health tracking, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is strictly for sleep tracking.

✅ You want a long battery life: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor can last up to eight nights on a single charge.

#3465. 46 Years Later, the Most Influential Thriller of All Time Is Officially Free on YouTube

There’s no better time to return to Camp Blood

There’s no better time to return to Camp Blood

Over the years, corporations and filmmakers alike have eagerly sought to revisit the origins of horror classics (e.g., Bates Motel and Psycho, Welcome to Derry and IT, etc.) for modern audiences. It’s an easy way to find successwhen you already have an audience that loves the IP you’re reimagining

Not even the Friday the 13th franchise has escaped the trend of revisiting the past. Crystal Lake, a new series from A24 and Peacock, follows Pamela Voorhees (Betsy Palmer), Jason Voorhees’s deranged mother​​​​​​​. It’s a prequel that, frankly, nobody really asked for (though we kind of liked it anyway), since Jason’s origins have already been explored: Sean S. Cunningham’s 1980s horror film Friday the 13th — available to watch now for free on YouTube.

Following the release of the genre-defining slasher Halloween, Cunningham and writer Victor Miller faced a real challenge: how to stand out in a subgenre flooded with horror movies (Black Christmas, Texas Chainsaw Massacre, to name just a few) trying to ride the slasher wave. Friday the 13th had to be memorable, interesting, and stand out.

On the surface, Friday the 13th doesn’t feel too different. It’s full of horny teens, heavy suspense, and a sense of isolation as a deranged killer hunts and kills them off, one by one. However, unlike other slashers like Halloween, Cunningham takes the brutality one step further by asking two very different but meaningful questions. Careful now, spoilers for a 46-year-old movie ahead.

First, what if the killer were not a man in a mask but a vengeful mother driven mad by society’s disregard for her disabled son? Second, what if Cunningham and Paramount hired Tom Savini, famous for his work on George A. Romero’s Dawn of the Dead, to create some of the most gruesome deaths audiences had yet seen on the silver screen?

The result is one of the bloodiest slashers of all time, one that shook up perceptions of how grotesque the horror subgenre could be and who, exactly, could be the one dealing out those kills in the first place.

Slashers like Halloween and Black Christmas have some gnarly kills—who could forget Michael Myers pinning Bob to a pantry door with a large knife or Barb being stabbed with a unicorn figurine’s horn? Savini, however, elevated Friday the 13th’s kills into a bloody art form with shocking, realistic gore.

Savini did more than deliver, too. Just as he used practical effects for Dawn of the Dead, he did so again for several of the film’s kills. One especially memorable kill is counselor Jack’s, in which he’s stabbed in the neck as he lies in bed. Using a prosthetic neck piece and a pump, fake blood was pumped to create a blood-spurt effect that, for its time, looked remarkably realistic.

The most significant thing that set Friday the 13th apart from its predecessors, however, was its killer: Pamela Voorhees. The slasher genre was no longer defined by masculine rage, but by a mother’s love. Even in the modern era of horror, slashers still feature far more male than female killers, but in 1980, Mrs. Voorhees was undoubtedly one of a kind.

Furthermore, for as deranged and murderous as she was, she exerted a strange, empathetic pull on audiences. Yes, murder is wrong — but you can’t deny that she loved her son. Unlike Michael Myers, who is often depicted as evil incarnate, Mrs. Voorhees has a complexity that made her brutal motives more compelling.

46 years later, Mrs. Voorhees's story begins anew with Crystal Lake. It’s unclear whether the series will get a second season, but even if it doesn’t, fans of Jason and his diabolical family tree needn’t worry. You can never go wrong with the original.

Friday the 13th is available to stream now for free on YouTube.

#3464. ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.]

At this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

In both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

For her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

But when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

De Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

When Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

She also picks up a new friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

Dani Kessel Odom (they/them) is an autistic lead writer and TV critic who covers sci-fi shows like Doctor Who and Pluribus, fantasy shows like The Magicians and Percy Jackson, and horror of all kinds. They also cover Marvel and DC TV shows and movies, with a robust knowledge of comic books. Their TV reviews can be found on Rotten Tomatoes.

Warning: This article includes mild SPOILERS for Percy Jackson & The Olympians season 3, episodes 1 & 2 and The Titan's Curse by Rick Riordan!

Camp Half-Blood might be the best-known group in the Riordanverse, but the Percy Jackson TV show has just introduced the Hunters of Artemis, a group that will play a significant role this season and return down the line. Percy Jackson & The Olympians has returned for a new season on Disney+, and the first two episodes of season 3 have already dropped. Each week, we’ll be treated to two episodes, which is a change from the past two seasons.

For the first time ever, the Percy Jackson book The Titan’s Curse has come to the screen. We’ve already met characters who are central to the story going forward. Bianca and Nico di Angelo were saved from the military school, where Annabeth was kidnapped, and they have made it to Camp Half-Blood. Atlas, Kronos’ right-hand man, is out from under the Titan’s curse, and he’s ready to help raise his fellow Titan. The most epic introduction so far, though, came from the Hunters of Artemis.

From their musical motif to the Hunters’ costumes, everything about their introduction was perfect, and they feel just as regal and dangerous as their book counterparts. The group will play a major role this season and again in Percy Jackson season 5, if Disney+ continues the show that far. Unfortunately, they didn’t give viewers much information about the Hunters of Artemis, and not everyone has read the books. If you’re wondering about the mysterious elite group, here’s everything you need to know about the group’s rules and structure and their motivations in the TV show.

The Hunters of Artemis are girls who pledge themselves to the goddess Artemis and join her on the Hunt. They serve as her companions, handmaids, and fellow hunters. Once they take the oath, they can’t live outside the Hunt. In the book, their oath is, “I pledge myself to the Goddess Artemis. I turn my back on the company of men, accept eternal maidenhood, and join the hunt.” We haven’t heard the vow in the TV show yet, as nobody has joined.

In the source material, the average age of the Hunters when they take the vow is around 12, and almost all are kids. However, they don’t have to be children, and they don’t have to be demigods. Instead, Artemis accepts any unmarried girl or woman, whether Half-Blood, human, nymph, or something else. The TV show ages the group up, making them look more like older teenagers.

A tangled mythic web of gods, Titans, and demigod, mapped into a clear visual for fans tracking family ties.

Upon joining, the Hunters become immortal with the caveat that they can die in battle. They stay frozen at the age they were when they joined unless they break their vow. On top of that benefit, when they take the vow, they get heightened strength, speed, agility, and archery precision. Each of them uses a specialized bow and arrow as a weapon. Technically, they are allowed to leave at any time, at which point they revert to the state they were in before they joined.

One of the changes Percy Jackson season 3 makes to The Titan’s Curse is the reason why the Hunters were at the military school when the Manticore attacks and their goal. In the book, they catch the Manticore's scent while hunting an ancient beast and follow it, hoping it’s the one they’ve been searching for. They may also have been in the area to recruit Annabeth, though this happens before the book starts.

However, Disney+’s Percy Jackson has them show up to protect Thalia and Percy, the Forbidden Children. They explicitly tell Annabeth that they aren’t there to get her answer about joining the Hunters. The reason she cares about Percy and Thalia is simple. Artemis knows the Great Prophecy, and she obviously doesn’t want Olympus to fall because that would be the end of her. Also, she knows the Bane of Olympus is back, which they’ve been hunting. Zoe tells Mr. D and the people at the camp that this creature can destroy Olympus if it devours a Forbidden Child.

As of Percy Jackson & The Olympians season 3 episodes 1 & 2, there’s no answer about who or what it looks like. I’m keeping spoilers mild in this article to preserve some of the big moments that could come up in the TV show. If you want to know what the Bane of Olympus is, it’s revealed in The Titan’s Curse chapter 15, “I Wrestle Santa’s Evil Twin,” on page 228.

Rather than just protect Thalia and Percy, Artemis orders her Hunters, led by Zoe, to confine the Forbidden Children inside Camp Half-Blood, even if the Oracle gives them a quest prophecy. Zoe takes this to the extreme, trying to tie them up in mental netting toward the end of Percy Jackson & The Olympians season 3, episode 2. The only reason they stop this plan is that the Oracle appears outside and reveals that Artemis has been kidnapped, and they can only save her with the help of Campers.

One of the best changes the Percy Jackson TV show makes is having Annabeth reveal to Percy that the Hunters of Artemis are recruiting her. This is a great way to lay the foundation for the group before they show up, and it also answers one of the book's biggest unanswered questions: why Annabeth considers joining. Fans have speculated about her logic for years, but the book never explains it. The only answer provided related to Annabeth and the Hunters is why she doesn’t join them in the end, which comes in The Demigod Files.

Annabeth explains to Percy, while dancing, that she can be used as a weapon against Percy and Thalia. She knows they would do anything to save her, bringing up Percy’s line, “If I had to choose between saving you or saving Olympus, Annabeth, I’d burn it all down.” If Annabeth joined the Hunters, she wouldn’t be around. Kronos and his goons could try to come get her from the Hunt, but Artemis and the other Hunters would protect her. Plus, she would have enhanced abilities.

Ultimately, her suspicion that others will use her to manipulate Percy and Thalia is correct. Atlas and Dr. Thorn kidnap Annabeth because they know that Percy and Thalia will come to rescue her. Kronos’ goons need the Forbidden Children and the Bane of Olympus to bring down Olympus, and they know that the two Campers won’t give up on Annabeth.

#3461. Amazon’s all-in-one cheap soundbar has a built-in subwoofer for under $250 — there's just one thing holding it back

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is an admirable entry-level soundbar. Although it won’t beat any of the big names unlike its cheaper sibling, the TV Soundbar, it provides an instant TV speaker upgrade without breaking the bank.

Built-in subwoofer with adjustable bass volume

Bass can overpower dialogue in action scenes

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Price: 4/5Sound quality: 3/5Design: 4/5Features: 3/5Overall score: 3.5/5Best for: The space-conscious, budget-conscious, subwoofer-wanters

All-in-one soundbars are a dangerous game. How does one balance center channels for dialogue with a subwoofer for the best blockbuster movie action? In the case of the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus, with semi-difficulty.

Don’t get me wrong, the price is incredibly appealing — $249 for a 3.1-channel soundbar is super affordable — and the minimalist design won’t cause any controversy. But is this enough to make it one of the best soundbars?

Yes and no. Unfortunately, the bass tends to overpower dialogue in action-heavy scenes. But could this still be the soundbar for you if you only watch TV and YouTube? Find out in this Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus review.

If you’re looking for a reason to buy the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus, that sweet, sweet MSRP is the biggest one.

At $249 at Amazon U.S. ($139 on sale) and £249 at Amazon U.K., the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus is incredibly cheap for what you get. It’s an all-in-one “Dolby Atmos” soundbar — yes, that means with a built-in subwoofer. The basic model, Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, is $119, so you’re essentially paying $130 for a built-in subwoofer.

At this price point, there’s very little competition. Of course, there’s the Samsung B750F ($297, 2025 model), which has a separate subwoofer and 5.1 channels (more upfiring speakers for better surround sound). Even so, this is $50 pricier, which can be a dealbreaker if you’re on a rigid budget.

I’ve also tested the Samsung Q600F — MSRP of $499 but often on sale in the $300s — which is 2025’s model but has a 3.1.2 channel setup, which is the minimum you need for genuine Dolby Atmos. I’ll get into this more below, but that’s the long and short of it.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349 with a 3.1 channel — so the same as the Amazon Plus and without the surround channels present on the Samsung Q600F — which I would recommend over the Plus if you have a little more to spare. Its separate subwoofer provides a stronger bass response without overpowering dialogue, unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus.

Like the $119 Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus model also has EQ modes. These are as follows: “Music”, “Movie”, “Sports”, and “Night”. There’s also individual bass level adjustment if you want to get really particular with your listening experience.

There's a dialogue mode, but this didn't isolate speech as well as I wanted it to, especially in louder, action-heavy scenes.

Music mode (connected via Bluetooth) is fine, although the bass was a little boomy and the vocals a little too sharp. I would recommend grabbing one of the best speakers, like the JBL Flip 7, to listen to music at home.

So let’s get one thing straight: the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus does not have “true” Dolby Atmos. If a soundbar doesn’t have side-firing or up-firing channel speakers, it physically cannot project soundwaves in that way.

In Top Gun: Maverick's dogfighting scene, I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV

However, the Plus has “Dolby Atmos”, which means it can technically decode Atmos signals. While this obviously doesn’t produce a genuinely immersive experience, it does have its moments. In the dogfighting scene in "Top Gun: Maverick," I could feel the soundtrack whoosh around me, and the radioed dialogue sounded as if it were coming from beside the TV. As I’ll get into later, this pushed the dialogue to the back of the soundstage, resulting in me straining to hear speech.

Dolby Atmos was better in “K-Pop Demon Hunters, which is really surprising. Usually, “Top Gun: Maverick” blows other movies out of the water in terms of Atmos. Cheering crowds were louder and more immersive in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," and some dialogue was positioned well in the up-firing speakers. One character's voice was particularly crisp and immersive — the lowest female voice — which makes me think the soundbar is better at isolating lower mids than sub-bass.

Despite having a range of EQ modes and a palatable price, unfortunately, the Plus gets a 3.5-star rating from me for a reason. There's one majorly important thing holding it back.

Unlike the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, the Plus really struggles to differentiate between dialogue and bass layers in action-heavy scenes. “Top Gun: Maverick” was particularly egregious here: Bass often overpowered dialogue, especially when the soundtrack was relatively heavy in flying scenes. I could barely hear Maverick's radioed dialogue to the characters in the control room over the string-heavy soundtrack and the flying airplane.

This was incredibly surprising, as the cheaper non-Plus model excelled in the very same scene. Bass volume was set to the minimum, and I watched on “Movie” mode.

While not as egregious in “K-Pop Demon Hunters," I still struggled to hear some dialogue. Surprisingly, the music sounded excellent in this movie, but dialogue is arguably the most important part. If you can’t hear the actors, what’s the point?

The consequences are really enormous: I struggled to make out dialogue in action-heavy scenes across the three movies I watched, which isn’t really what you want when using a soundbar. The whole purpose of a soundbar is to make dialogue more intelligible.

However, I also watched "Gilmore Girls" on basic Netflix, which sounded great. If you predominantly watch TV or YouTube, I don't think you'll notice this issue. It's just a concern for action movie buffs. In that case, I'd recommend checking out the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375).

At $249, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is incredibly affordable. There are very few soundbars that can beat this in terms of penny-per-performance.

The aforementioned Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is $349, so $100 more than the Amazon model, but has a dedicated subwoofer and a center channel for dialogue. I would personally save up more and buy the Sony model over the Amazon.

But if I were to save more money, I'd choose the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar (non-Plus) over the Plus version. Sure, there's no subwoofer, but it's just $119 and genuinely sounds fantastic. It's the best budget soundbar I've ever tested.

Hmm. This is a tricky one. I loved the basic Amazon Fire TV Soundbar — if you want seriously great sound at a low price, get that one. The extra $130 for the Plus model? Not worth it, if you ask me. I would either spend an extra $50 on the Samsung B750F or an extra $130 on the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer.

Unfortunately, due to a lack of communication between the built-in subwoofer and the main channel speakers, dialogue can be overpowered during action-heavy scenes. Consequently, I can’t recommend this model over the Samung B750F. Personally, I would either get the cheaper Amazon Fire TV Soundbar or the aforementioned Samsung model. Or, you could save up a little extra for the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus with Subwoofer ($375) or the with Rears version ($489).

However, if you have an Amazon Fire TV and want something capable of integrating into the ecosystem seamlessly (even though you'll need a separate Fire stick or Fire TV), without having to spend an extra $50 on the B750F, the Plus is a great deal.

#3460. Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026

““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. It’s a big improvement on the last “Hunger Games” prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which made $5.75 million in previews and kicked off with $44 million. That film would gross over $166 million domestically and nearly $364 million globally, figures that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is on pace to easily eclipse.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel of the same name. It tells the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy, the alcoholic former Hunger Games victor played by Woody Harrelson in the films. The sequel checks in with him at 16 as he’s forced to compete in gladiatorial combat. “East of Eden” breakout Joseph Zada plays Haymitch. He’s surrounded by an all-star cast that includes Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, and Maya Hawke. Francis Lawrence, who helmed most of the series’ films, returns as director. Lionsgate, which is having a strong year at the box office thanks to “Michael,” is backing the “Hunger Games” sequel as it has the previous films.

The biggest competition for “Sunrise on the Reaping” this weekend isn’t another major movie, but the release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” which is expected to be a phenomenon.

#3459. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

Proper balance becomes crucial in your senior years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As a certified personal trainer, I work with a wide range of clients who have lots of different fitness goals. But for my clients in their 60s and beyond, there’s usually one objective that drives their training: improving balance and stability.

I recently started working with a 60-year-old client who wanted to focus on just that. She noticed that she was a little more unsteady on her feet than she used to be, and had a few close calls with falling. After a thorough check-up with her doctor, we began our work together with the following routine.

These exercises aren’t just for seniors. It’s never too early to start thinking about your balance, so give them a try during your next workout. They’re appropriate for any fitness level and you won’t need any equipment to do them (but adding a dumbbell or two will always make things more challenging).

Check in with your doctor before trying any new workout, especially if you have balance concerns.

These exercises aren’t hard, but doing them correctly is important. Beginners should consider meeting with a personal trainer or physical therapist for feedback and guidance on form, and to get modifications if needed.

You’ll just need some room and an elevated platform, like a stair step, for this workout. Hang onto a chair or another stable surface for additional support if you need it.

Start by doing each exercise for one set of 10 reps. As your balance improves, you can add an additional set and increase your reps to 12. You can also use small dumbbells for the step-up to balance to ramp up the difficulty.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

These exercises can be done on their own or as a warm-up for other activities.

You may feel muscle fatigue when doing this workout, but you should never feel sharp pain. Stop the workout immediately and consult your physician if you feel sharp pain at any point.

The exercises in this workout force you to find equilibrium when your center of gravity is maintained over a smaller surface area – either one foot for the standing marches, step up to balance, and side step to balance, or a narrow placement of two feet for the heel-to-toe walks.

During these exercises, your deep core muscles like the rectus abdominis and internal obliques engage to stabilize and support your entire body. Your glutes and hip stabilizing muscles also work to keep the hips in a level position. The stronger these muscles are, the more conditioned they’ll be to keep you upright and sturdy during everyday movement.

Additionally, exercises like the step-up to balance strengthen key muscle groups in your lower body, like the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes.

#3456. ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 New York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.]

Paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of new love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy New York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.)

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its New York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the New York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

#3454. What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole new task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro said. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”

In addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro said. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and said, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”
