#3431. ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he said. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

#3430. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

Last Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console.

Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games:

Donkey Kong Bananza was one of Nintendo's launch titles for the Switch 2. And while it's been out for over a year, Donkey Kong's first 3D game is still among the best-reviewed titles on the console. Nintendo is taking $30 off the game's MSRP for this promotion.

Kirby Air Riders on Switch 2 is only the second installment in the series. The original launched all the way back on the GameCube, and while the title typically runs for $69.99, Nintendo is letting it go for $39.99.

Metroid Prime 4 arrived last year after an 18-year wait from Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. The game typically retails between $59.99 and $69.99 for a physical copy, but Nintendo is selling it for $39.99 during its early Black Friday promotion.

Super Mario Galaxy (both the original and the sequel) are beloved by fans. These titles originally launched on the Wii, and Nintendo rereleased both for the Switch. (The company offers a free upgrade to the Switch 2 edition.) Nintendo asks $69.99 for this combo, and while you can find it for under $60, you'll officially be able to pick it up for $39.99 before Black Friday.

Nintendo's latest Mario Party, Jamboree, has a Switch 2 edition with a rather staggering MSRP of $79.99. While it's the version of the game with the most features, it's also the most expensive. You'll be able to buy it for $39.99 for Black Friday, saving up to $40.

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale. Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

It depends! Its Nintendo Switch 2 bundle deal runs from Nov. 22 through Dec. 5; the select games listed above will be on sale from Nov. 22 through Nov. 29; and digital titles will have discounts from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2.

While we don't know which digital titles will be discounted yet, we do know that physical copies of Donkey Kong Bananza, Kirby Air Riders, Metroid Prime 4: Beyond, Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2, and Super Mario Party: Jamboree will be on sale for $39.99 each.

Yes! The Switch 2 alone costs $499.99, so you essentially get the game for free. Mario Kart World is also one of the console's best multiplayer titles right now, so it makes sense to pick it up in this bundle.

#3429. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#3428. Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

Trump mentioned Georgia and New Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”

Trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors announced more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he said, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she said in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”

A floor vote has yet to be announced, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

#3427. Now These Apple Services Are Down

If you're having trouble accessing certain Apple products and services today, you are not alone. As of early Tuesday afternoon, Downdetector shows user reports of issues across multiple Apple services. While Apple's System Status page initially showed far fewer issues than Downdetector users reported, the site has since updated to reflect general outages.

According to users on Downdetector, there are currently outages or interruptions to the following Apple services, in order of most to least reported: Apple Support, Apple Pay, iCloud, App Store, Apple Business Manager, Apple Music, Apple Store, Sign In with Apple, Apple Card. As of 1:44 p.m., Apple Support had the most reports, with over 13,000 user complaints. Comments suggest that users cannot log into their iCloud accounts, Apple Accounts, or activate devices, among other issues.

According to Apple, the disruptions aren't quite as widespread: Apple says that the App Store, Apple Music, AppleCare on Devices, and Schoolwork are all experiencing outages. Apple says that the App Store and Apple Music "may be slow or unavailable," while AppleCare purchase is currently unavailable. The company's System Status page shows an "issue" with iCloud Account & Sign In. Other services with user reports on Downdetector, including the Apple Card, Apple Online Store, and Apple Business, read as "Available." Apple also says there was an outage with the Volume Purchase Program, but that has since been resolved.

It's not clear what's causing the issues with the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud Account & Sign In, or other Apple services at this time. However, the timing is odd. It comes after a number of banks experienced outages on Monday, as well as Microsoft's massive outage the previous week. In addition to all of these outages, the FAA unexpectedly grounded all U.S. flights on Friday, for only the third time in the agency's history.

#3426. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

#3425. DC's Next Batman Was Never Going To Be Nightwing

On the surface, Dick Grayson's Nightwing may seem like an obvious choice to one day succeed Batman and don the cape and cowl. After all, he was The Dark Knight's very first Robin and oldest adopted son. However, DC Comics has spent quite some time establishing a much different trajectory for Grayson, while setting up someone else entirely to one day become the next Caped Crusader.

In the past, Dick Grayson had indeed filled in as Batman in Bruce Wayne's absence. However, it's one thing to become a temporary Dark Knight or for the comics to showcase an alt-reality "What If?" type scenario (see DC K.O. Knightfight), and quite another to suggest that Nightwing will one day become a full-time Batman for the foreseeable future. That's never going to be in the cards for several reasons.

Ever since he left Robin behind, Dick's evolution into Nightwing has long been punctuated by the desire to be more than Batman and step out of his shadow. Conversely, DC Comics clearly has someone else in mind to become the next Batman, and he's already been wearing the cape and cowl: Jace Fox.

Dick Grayson has successfully taken over as Batman before, most notably after Bruce Wayne's apparent death in Final Crisis. This era saw Dick becoming a new Batman alongside Damian Wayne as his Robin in the critically acclaimed Batman and Robin run. As such, it's been proven that Dick can and has become The Dark Knight when needed (but that doesn't mean he should long-term).

When he left his role as Robin behind, Dick Grayson's decision to become Nightwing was all about creating a new identity all his own, beyond Bruce. This included his move to Gotham's sister city of Blüdhaven. In the several years that have followed, Dick has become an A-list DC hero in his own right in the modern era, leading the Titans and protecting his own city without needing Batman's name or reputation.

Perhaps even more importantly, Bruce himself has indicated that he wants something far better for his eldest son (and all his sons) than simply becoming another Batman in his stead. Likewise, Dick Grayson has retained so much more of his optimism and brightness, choosing to move past his own parents' deaths rather than Bruce and his ongoing struggle to do just that.

Rather than asking him to ever take his place full-time, Bruce Wayne has every reason to want Dick to continue being Nightwing and prove that the next generation can become something greater than Batman himself. He already knows (and has said) that Dick is a far greater hero as Nightwing than he'll ever be as Batman. As such, wanting Dick to become Batman would undermine several years of development and crucial storytelling for both characters and their relationship.

Timothy "Jace" Fox, the estranged son of Lucius Fox, is a far more interesting possibility. First introduced as the next Batman in DC's Future State initiative, Jace received a proper present-day origin in The Next Batman: Second Son, exploring his complicated history and years away from his family. When he came back to Gotham, Jace chose to take up Batman's mantle, using advanced armor to fight as a secondary Dark Knight before eventually moving to New York City.

As seen in I Am Batman, the series explored what a new character could do with the mantle of The Dark Knight outside Gotham itself. At the same time, Jace's connection to Lucius still kept him connected to many of the resources associated with Bruce Wayne's crusade.

Keeping that in mind, the upcoming Batman: Reign of Assassins series is particularly exciting. Releasing in 2027, the five-issue series reunites writer John Ridley and artist Olivier Coipel, bringing Jace and Bruce together for their first true ongoing team-up, which should no doubt provide some brand-new explorations into their dynamics as simultaneous Batmen.

All things considered, DC Comics absolutely intends to use Jace to continue examining what the Batman legacy looks like in a new generation, and it will be SO much better than Dick Grayson ever becoming a permanent next Dark Knight.

Batman: Reign of Assassins #1 is available February 27 from DC Comics

#3423. iOS 27.3’s redesigned Apple Health app requires newer iPhone model

iOS 27.3 will introduce an all-new Apple Health experience when it ships next month, but you’ll need an AI-compatible iPhone to get it. Here’s why.

When iOS 27.3 launches next month, it will include a variety of upgrades for Apple TV, Apple Music, Siri AI, iCloud+, the iPhone Duo, and more.

Another tentpole addition is an all-new Apple Health app, which was first unveiled back in September when new Apple Watch models debuted.

The Health app is getting a full revamp in iOS 27.3 that’s meant to be more personalized and informative than ever. New features include an Insights tab, Longevity tab, educational videos, at-home movement evaluations, and more.

But for many iPhone users who update to iOS 27.3, the Health app might remain largely unchanged. Why? Because the new experience relies on Apple Intelligence, so you’ll need an AI-compatible iPhone to get it.

That means an iPhone 15 Pro or newer is required.

If you have an older iPhone model, or simply have chosen not to enable Apple Intelligence on your device, you’ll miss out on the new Health features. They’ll also only be available in select languages initially.

These forthcoming Health upgrades join the 20+ other new Apple Intelligence features that recently debuted in iOS 27.

Have you tried the new Health app in iOS 27.3? How is it working for you? Let us know in the comments.

#3422. If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It

The uproar over the alleged use of generative AI imagery in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has taken a familiar path. Early responses to the Netflix film penned by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher have pointed out egregious examples of generative video artifacts sticking out in key flashback moments in the film — including one shot from the trailer where it certainly looks like a video AI program rendered a wagon the wrong way around.

The criticism is of the use of generative AI in principle as a fundamental betrayal of the creative process — but it’s also of Fincher, as a director who, historically, has been meticulous with the level of detail and intention in every single shot of his films. In the early responses to Fincher’s latest, there’s been a lot of surprise and disappointment about this particular filmmaker being caught up in an AI controversy. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

At first blush, his approach seems at odds with using generative AI video, which relies on regurgitated (and, it bears repeating every time, stolen) data. But Fincher has defended his use of AI to the LA Times as a way to continue to innovate on an art form that is, after all, just over a hundred years old.

That defense really shouldn’t be surprising, given Fincher’s history with AI specifically. Although he’s been critical of generative tools in the past, Fincher admitted to using them (never publicly disclosing which) in the 4K remaster of “Se7en,” which the director described as a process of needing to remake the negative in order to battle the ravages of time (and the thousands of tiny scratches that would show up in 4K). “If you could see a 30-year-old negative and what it looks like even when immaculately stored — it was an enormous amount of fixing, just digs and scratches and cinch,” he told EW at the time.

That kind of image restoration technology was around long, long before the Anthropic IPO failed to save the stock market, but its level of precision has increased enormously in the past year. There were also sequences in the stored “Se7en,” though, where generative tech filled in gaps from the original. For one example, Fincher talked about a moment where a camera pan overshot the mark and changedh a shot. The performance had been good enough to use a technically flawed take — and, combined wit an unused take, allowed software to generate the missing information and restore the intended image.

“It ends up being the most thrillingly stupid fix in the world because if you see it, we didn’t do our jobs. And you probably won’t see it. You probably won’t be aware that it’s happened. But you look at it, and you just think to yourself, ‘It’s so nice that we can fix that kind of stuff today,'” Fincher told Collider about that moment in “Se7en.”

By Fincher’s own lights, then, the problem with AI in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is that people are painfully aware of it. AI critics might make a distinction between video restoration tools that work on existing projects and those tools being used because they can more quickly and cheaply generate originals that would’ve otherwise needed to be crafted by human hands. Having something AI-generated isn’t necessarily better than nothing when it comes to art, and choosing to AI-generate a Western chase sequence inside of, say, 10 seconds isn’t a solution to all.

Still, Fincher knows what he’s doing. This past week, he emphasized to the LA Times that he’s not a Luddite when it comes to film: “We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old, and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?”

The answer is an emphatic “No!” to some And they can certainly be mad, or disappointed, or disheartened about Fincher’s decision to use AI tools. The one thing they shouldn’t be is surprised.

#3419. Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

The Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow arrived in a clear plastic bag within a cardboard box. It wasn’t vacuum sealed, meaning when I pulled it out of the plastic bag, it was ready to be slept on.

I can sleep on my side with the standard loft size. However, I think the high loft would be better if I was strictly a side sleeper.

When the pillow eventually breaks down, I can see myself sleeping on my side less and less with this pillow and reverting to my back or stomach. Those with broad shoulders should choose the high loft size from the get-go.

I placed a 15lb weight in the center of the pillow, and it sunk over an inch. That makes sense considering the foams inside are shredded. When I lifted the dumbbell, the pillow sprung back into shape immediately, which is a good sign of the its durability.

I didn’t wake up hot or sweaty when sleeping on the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow, and that’s all thanks to Saatva’s temperature regulation. Memory foam is a far more heat-retaining material than natural latex, so to mitigate any overheating issues, Saatva utilized organic cotton for the cover — which is breathable — and shredded the memory foam and latex interior fill so air could weave its way through and keep my temperature neutral at night.

During the beginning of testing, I was sleeping without the air-conditioner and just a fan, so it was about 75 degrees in my house when I fell asleep at night and around 70 degrees when I woke up in the morning. The fact that heat did not build up during that time was very promising, and most likely what you can expect throughout the year.

A good rule of thumb: replace your pillows every two years and keep an eye on how quickly your pillow bounces back over time.

This can be done by folding your pillow in half. A slow bounce back means the fill has worn down. Until the pillow breaks down, maintenance will ensure it lasts longer.

During the testing period, the Saatva Cloud Memory Foam Pillow bounced back quickly, leading us to believe that it’ll last the full two years of a pillow's lifetime. Especially if you wash the cover consistently.

All in all, this supportive and huggable pillow will cradle your head and lead to a comfortable night’s sleep.

#3417. Report: iPhone set to gain market share in 2027 amid industry-wide slump

Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a new report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a new Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That said, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less important in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

#3415. Michael Connelly Finally Gives Us The Bosch Backstory We’ve Been Waiting For In New Release

This article contains mention of child abuse.

For over 30 years, Bosch has been a standout thriller series, and the author, Michael Connelly, hasn't stopped surprising readers. In his new release, Connelly delves further into the background and origin of the protagonist, Harry Bosch, than ever, shedding new light on his development.

When audiences first met Bosch in the 1992 novel, The Black Echo, Connelly introduced us to the world of the LAPD homicide detective and the cases he solves. Of course, things quickly get personal for Bosch as his background as a soldier in the Vietnam War and troubled past influence how he solves some grisly murders in Los Angeles. The Bosch TV show has done an amazing job bringing Connelly's novels to life, but it's always exciting when the writer adds texture to his backstory in the novels.

The most recent Bosch book, The Hollow, was released this past year in October 2026, and is the 26th volume in the Bosch franchise. Though Harry Bosch has come a long way since his early days solving crimes for the LAPD, Connelly keeps raising the bar, finding new ways to expand his story and crafting unbelievable thrillers that readers can't put down. Currently rated at 4.48 stars on Goodreads, The Hollow debuted to a warm reception because it takes us back to the beginning of Bosch's history.

Of course, readers know that Harry Bosch hasn't always had the easiest life, and Connelly has explored his past before, but The Hollow goes further than ever before, digging into Bosch's childhood. Just because Bosch retired from the LAPD, his time stopping criminals is far from over, and in the 2026 book, it's more emotional than ever. The Hollow touches upon Bosch's experience as a ward of the state as a child in the wake of his mother's murder.

His half-brother, Mickey Haller, tells Bosch that MacLaren Children’s Center, where Bosch suffered abuse as a child, has finally been busted in a class-action lawsuit, and Bosch is entitled to a huge settlement. However, money isn't what interests Bosch. Though he's tried to hide from this dark period of his past for a long time, Bosch is determined to solve the long-cold case of a child, Chops, he knew at MacLaren, who was found dead.

With his investigative skills and the fact that he can no longer pretend that Chops' death doesn't haunt him, Bosch has all the fuel he needs to track down the predator whom he believes killed Chops. The central villain in The Hollow is a shocking antagonist, making Bosch's investigation all the more compelling as he closes in on him. However, the most arresting part of The Hollow isn't the case, but Bosch's arc coming to grips with the abuse he faced as a child.

Harry Bosch will face something truly tragic in Michael Connelly's next Bosch book, and readers should prepare to see him in an entirely new light.

The Hollow is an emotional, intense book and one of Connelly's most cathartic, as the novel pulls no punches when it comes to bringing Bosch face to face with some of the most traumatic moments of his childhood. The Bosch franchise has always touched upon heavy themes, as Connelly's thriller novels explore dark criminal cases and murders. However, the personal element of The Hollow, and the way Bosch grows as a character throughout the story, make it a worthy addition to Connelly's work.

It makes sense that reviews of The Hollow have been positive, as it satisfies longtime fans who were hoping to get deeper insight into Bosch and his background. Though it's not the best place to start when beginning the Bosch novels, The Hollow was a vital addition to the canon and will be remembered as a pivotal volume that changed the way we see Harry Bosch forever.

#3414. WhatsApp’s first-party chat history backup service moves ahead

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Users can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app update.

#3413. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

#3412. iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

#3411. 8 Books Like Harry Potter, but Better

It is an undeniable fact that the Harry Potter novels are among the most influential book series of all time. With over 600 million copies sold worldwide, J.K. Rowling’s fantasy novels have made an indelible mark on the genre, shaping both literature and global culture. That said, just because it’s the best-selling book series of all time doesn’t mean it’s the best book series of all time.

There have been several great fantasy books released over the decades that share similarities with Harry Potter but deliver much better stories and experiences. Not all of them have achieved comparable levels of fame and success, but their quality and significance to the genre are undeniable. With that in mind, here’s our selection of books that are like Harry Potter, but better.

Ursula K. Le Guin’s A Wizard of Earthsea is a classic fantasy novel that’s widely credited with establishing the magical academy setting later used in the Harry Potter series. Set in the titular archipelago, the book follows Ged, a young and impulsive mage who accidentally unleashes a shadow into the world. Haunted by this shadow, Ged sets off on a journey, mastering his powers and gaining deeper wisdom to confront it.

A Wizard of Earthsea may have a few cosmetic similarities to Harry Potter, but the novel exists on a whole other level, taking a philosophical approach to magic that’s about a lot more than magic duels and good vs. evil. A pioneering work of modern fantasy, the book won the 1969 Boston Globe-Horn Book Award and was one of the final recipients of the Lewis Carroll Shelf Award in 1979. It’s had a strong influence on the fantasy genre ever since and was followed by five more books that collectively make up the Earthsea Cycle.

The debut novel of Irish playwright Derek Landy, Skulduggery Pleasant (also known as Skulduggery Pleasant: Scepter of the Ancients or simply The Scepter of the Ancients), is the first book of the novel series. A genre-bending urban fantasy mystery, the book introduces the young Stephanie Edgley, who inherits her late uncle’s estate and soon finds herself targeted by the forces of a dangerous necromancer. Thankfully, she gets some magical help from the titular mage, a skeleton detective/wizard.

Skulduggery Pleasant was quite favorably received at the time of its publication and went on to win the Red House Children's Book Award and the Hampshire Book Award, as well as several other accolades. It’s an engaging dark fantasy that easily rivals Harry Potter for entertainment, blending horror, mystery, and fantasy, with a relatable protagonist and a fascinating cast of interesting characters. The novel has since spawned a massive series that includes 27 books, the latest, A Small Matter of Impending Catastrophe, released in 2025.

One of the books most commonly recommended to fans of Harry Potter, Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief is the first novel in Rick Riordan’s bestselling Camp Half-Blood Chronicles franchise. The book introduces readers to 12-year-old Percy Jackson, the demigod son of the Greek god Poseidon, who discovers the secret of his parentage just in time to be caught in the middle of a potential war. His only option to prevent this catastrophe is to head out on a cross-country quest alongside his friends, Annabeth Chase and Grover Underwood.

Witty, energetic, and highly endearing, The Lightning Thief is a fun take on Greek mythology that takes audiences into the fascinating world of ancient gods and monsters. It’s an engaging coming-of-age fantasy novel and a great entry point into the Camp Half-Blood Chronicles, which has since evolved into a massive world. The novel was adapted as a 2010 film by Chris Columbus and more recently adapted for the Disney+ series Percy Jackson and the Olympians, co-created by Riordan.

The first novel of Eoin Colfer’s book series, Artemis Fowl is a young adult fantasy novel centered on the titular character, a 12-year-old criminal mastermind. With the assistance of his loyal bodyguard Butler, Artemis sets out to capture an elf police officer, setting off a major hostage crisis in the fairy world. The book was followed by ten sequels split across two cycles.

Since its publication in 2001, Artemis Fowl has been highly acclaimed by critics and very popular with readers, developing a sizable fanbase. Combining a sharp sense of humor with intelligent plotting, the book and the series it spawned are easily among the best of 21st-century fantasy, with the series selling more than 21 million copies around the world. A film based on the novel was released in 2020 to highly negative reviews, but though that adaptation was a failure, an animated series is currently in development.

First published in Germany in 2003, Inkheart is a young adult fantasy novel by Cornelia Funke that’s the first book in the series. The novel follows Meggie, a young girl who lives with her father Mortimer, a bookbinder. A visit by a strange man named Dustfinger upends Meggie's and Mortimer’s lives, and Meggie learns that her father has a rare ability to conjure things out of books by reading aloud from them.

A fascinating fantasy book that’s partly a coming-of-age story and partly a celebration of storytelling, Inkheart was quite favorably received at the time of its publication. The novel became a finalist for the 2004 BookSense Book of the Year Award for Children's Literature and won other accolades as well. The book was followed by three sequels, 2005’s Inkspell, 2007’s Inkdeath, and 2023’s The Colour of Revenge, and a film adaptation was released in 2008.

A cozy fantasy romance novel written by Sangu Mandanna, The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches centers on young witch Mika Moon. The story is set in a world where witches live in secrecy and isolation. Born (and orphaned) in India but now living in the UK, Mika deals with her loneliness by making fake roleplay videos where she “pretends” to be a witch, but when someone recognizes her magic as real, Mika finds herself caring for three young witches living with non-magical adults in a place called Nowhere House.

Sangu Mandanna's earlier books before The Very Secret Society of Irregular Witches were all middle-grade and young adult fiction, and the novel is her adult debut. As such, the book is suited to a more mature audience than the average Harry Potter reader, but it is a great read for adults who grew up dreaming of Hogwarts. There’s no magical school, and the conflicts of the book are more interpersonal than world-ending, but it’s a delightful read that’s as cozy and warm as a Studio Ghibli movie.

Lev Grossman’s The Magicians is the first book of the new adult fantasy trilogy of the same name. The novel is centered on Quentin Coldwater, a young high school graduate who grew up reading a Chronicles of Narnia-esque book series set in a magical world called Fillory. After he is accepted into a secret magical college, Quentin discovers that Fillory and its magic are real — and a lot more dangerous than he thought.

Often compared to Harry Potter, The Magicians’ first and most obvious distinction is that its magical school is a university, where magical studies involve a lot less wand-waving and a lot more actual studying. Beyond that, the book and its sequels explore significantly more complex and delightfully weird concepts that are highly engaging for fans of modern fantasy. A TV adaptation premiered on Syfy in 2015, and The Magicians was followed by two sequels, 2011’s The Magician King and 2014’s The Magician’s Land, as well as two comic book series.

Written by Philip Pullman, His Dark Materials is a dark fantasy trilogy that consists of 1995’s Northern Lights (published as The Golden Compass in North America), 1997’s The Subtle Knife, and 2000’s The Amber Spyglass. The first book introduces the central character, Lyra Belacqua, a young child from a universe where people’s souls manifest outside their bodies as animal companions. Lyra’s adventures bring her into conflict with the theocratic rulers of her world, the Magisterium, as she learns more about the nature of the mysterious multiversal substance known as Dust.

Combining parallel universes and dark matter with fantasy concepts and a compelling coming-of-age story, His Dark Materials is a class apart from other fantasy books. A true fantasy masterpiece, the trilogy has earned critical acclaim and won several accolades, including the Carnegie Medal. The books have inspired multiple adaptations, including a 2007 film and a BBC-HBO TV series, and the original trilogy was followed by four short works and a sequel trilogy, the latest of which is 2025’s The Rose Field.

Of these, I have read inkheart, Percy jackson, and his dark materials, and I can say that in my opinion, none of them is better than Harry Potter. They are all really good, but they all have plot holes and plot inconsistencies on a level that just doesn't exist in the Harry Potter universe because those books were so well thought out. My feelings about JK Rowling's views aside, they are just Superior books. Not that they don't have any plot holes, they just aren't as egregious. There is never a point where a fact is laid out about a character, and then three books later is set aside and the opposite is said to be true. That happens a lot in other book series.

#3409. Fallout 5 Official Release Update Shared By Bethesda And Microsoft

It was actually quite an exciting moment earlier this year when Bethesda finally broke cover to give us updates on basically everything they have going on right now. That meant that we finally know what's going on with Fallout, The Elder Scrolls, and even Starfield, if anyone is still invested in how that plays out in the future.

For Fallout in particular, we got a ton of exciting information, including confirmation that both Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas were getting the remakes that had been rumored for a long time. In addition, Fallout 5 was also confirmed to be entering full development, though given the protracted cycles of AAA games, the crushing reality is that it's likely still a long way away from being made available to players.

Though things have been relatively quiet since, there has now been an update and it further cements exactly what we though the situation was going to be.

As first reported by GameRant, Bethesda has now reiterated to fans that Fallout 5 remains their "long-term destination," and it will likely be the last of the previously announced projects to arrive in our laps.

The story of Fallout 5 up to this point has been one of frustratingly little progress, particularly given how big the studio is. Todd Howard first spoke about the game all the way back in 2018 (now known as the cursed year), when he simply confirmed that it would be a single-player effort. He then went on to confirm that they had a one-pager for the game in 2021, before he confirmed a year later that it would be their next big project after The Elder Scrolls VI.

Back then, there would have been plenty of players out there who were expecting to be playing The Elder Scrolls VI by now, but that obviously isn't the case. In fact, it would be a major surprise if we are playing it before 2028, which likely means that Fallout 5 is going to be considerably further away, well into the 2030s.

The only potential silver lining to that timeline is that new Xbox head Asha Sharma has made it very clear that she wants Fallout to be at the center of the company's strategy moving forward. Possibly motivated by the success of the Prime Video adaptation, it may well be that additional resources are moved across to get the game out sooner.

At the same time, those remakes we mentioned earlier should also be along much sooner than that, allowing us to explore two of the better RPGs of all-time in brand-new fidelity. Though we don't have dates just yet, 2027 does seem like a reasonable estimate for the first of those, finally giving us something to do with the franchise while we wait.

At the same time, the third season of Fallout on Prime Video has wrapped filming, and that will definitely debut next year, most likely in the months around June. If that's anywhere near as good as fans are expecting, then things could be relatively positive from here on out for fans of the franchise.

Fallout is a post-apocalyptic RPG franchise set in an alternate future where a nuclear war devastates the world. Players explore vast, open worlds filled with mutants, raiders, and advanced technology. The series emphasizes player choice, allowing various approaches to combat, dialogue, and decision-making. Each game follows different protagonists navigating the wasteland to uncover secrets, form alliances, and rebuild civilization amidst the ruins of the old world. The franchise is known for its rich lore, dark humor, and retro-futuristic aesthetic, which has transferred over into its new series on Amazon Prime.

#3408. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3407. Apple announces App Store price changes in multiple countries, new California tax rules

Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today announced a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the company, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”

Apple added that a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and update their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”

#3406. The UK and some other countries don’t get more Siri AI usage with iCloud+

Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB plan to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances …

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud plans.

However, tucked away in the small print in the company’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

What’s your take? Please share your thoughts in the comments.
